articles.title: After 30 years, scientists finally have a drug for a deadly brain disease
articles.text:
After 30 years, scientists finally have a drug for a deadly brain disease
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- University of Wisconsin-Madison
- Summary:
- The FDA has approved the first drug that directly targets Alexander disease, a devastating neurological disorder affecting fewer than one in a million people. Developed through decades of research, Zanvastro showed promising results in clinical trials, stabilizing motor function and even improving movement in some patients.
- Share:
The FDA has approved the first drug designed to directly treat Alexander disease, an extremely rare neurological disorder that progressively damages the nervous system and can be fatal. The treatment, called Zanvastro, represents a major advance for patients who previously had no options beyond managing their symptoms.
Alexander disease can interfere with movement, thinking, and automatic bodily functions such as breathing and heart rate. Zanvastro is the first and only approved disease-modifying treatment for the condition, meaning it targets an underlying biological process responsible for the disease rather than simply relieving its effects.
The drug emerged from more than three decades of scientific research at the University of Wisconsin-Madison's School of Veterinary Medicine and Waisman Center. Much of that work took place in the laboratory of Albee Messing, professor emeritus of comparative biosciences and former director of the Waisman Center, whose discoveries helped make the treatment possible. Ionis Pharmaceuticals collaborated in developing the drug.
Clinical trials offered encouraging results. Patients receiving Zanvastro generally experienced stabilization of their motor function, and some showed improvements in their ability to move.
"This is a wonderful and long-awaited day for the Alexander disease community," Messing says.
Alexander Disease: A Rare and Devastating Brain Disorder
Alexander disease affects fewer than one in every million people worldwide. Although exceptionally uncommon, its consequences can be severe, with symptoms that gradually interfere with everyday activities and essential bodily functions.
People with the disorder may develop seizures, lose previously acquired developmental abilities, experience increasing difficulty walking or moving, and struggle with speaking or swallowing. Some also develop dangerously elevated pressure inside the brain.
The disease does not follow a single predictable course. Symptoms may first emerge during infancy, childhood, or adulthood, and their severity and progression can differ depending on when the condition begins.
For decades, doctors could offer supportive care and treatments to ease individual symptoms, but they had no approved medication capable of targeting the disease itself.
An Unexpected Discovery Revealed the Genetic Cause
The breakthrough can be traced to research Messing conducted with Michael Brenner, professor emeritus of neurobiology at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. In the late 1990s, their work identified the genetic changes responsible for Alexander disease, providing scientists with a specific biological target for developing treatments.
The discovery began with an unexpected result in laboratory mice.
Messing and Brenner had genetically engineered mice to produce unusually high amounts of a protein known as glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). This protein is normally found in astrocytes, specialized cells that help support and maintain healthy function in the brain and spinal cord.
To the researchers' surprise, the modified mice developed abnormal protein deposits throughout their brains. These deposits appeared inside astrocytes and closely resembled the distinctive abnormalities seen in people with Alexander disease.
"We had, really without intending to, created a mouse that produced these classic lesions of Alexander disease," Messing says.
The abnormal deposits, called Rosenthal fibers, are a defining characteristic of the disorder. Additional genetic studies involving people diagnosed with Alexander disease confirmed that mutations in the gene responsible for producing GFAP were the underlying cause.
"This provided an obvious and specific strategy for therapy -- the GFAP protein," Messing explains.
Identifying the genetic cause also made diagnosing the condition much simpler. Instead of relying on invasive brain biopsies to look for characteristic tissue abnormalities, doctors could use genetic testing from a blood sample to identify the mutations associated with the disease.
Scientists Develop a Drug That Targets Harmful Protein Buildup
Once researchers understood the role of GFAP, their next challenge was finding a way to reduce its production and prevent damaging levels of the protein from accumulating in brain cells.
Messing joined forces with Tracy Hagemann, an associate research professor at the Waisman Center, to create improved rodent models of Alexander disease. These models more closely reproduced important features of the disorder, giving scientists a way to investigate potential treatments before testing them in people.
The team focused on a straightforward idea: If excessive GFAP contributes to the disease, lowering the amount produced might help protect the nervous system.
In collaboration with Ionis Pharmaceuticals, the researchers pursued a technology known as antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs).
These treatments use short, specially designed pieces of genetic material to interfere with instructions that cells use to manufacture particular proteins. Rather than targeting every protein in a cell, an ASO can be designed to reduce production of a specific one.
For Alexander disease, that target was GFAP.
The experimental treatment produced promising results in rodents, supporting the decision to move forward with human testing. A clinical trial began in the summer of 2021.
Zanvastro uses this same targeted strategy. By limiting GFAP production, the drug aims to reduce the buildup of the protein before it can cause additional damage.
Because the treatment needs to reach the central nervous system, it is administered through an injection into the spinal canal. A trained healthcare professional gives the injection once every three months.
Clinical Trials Show Improvements in Walking and Movement
The human trial provided evidence that lowering GFAP could offer meaningful benefits to people living with Alexander disease.
Ionis Pharmaceuticals conducted the international study across 13 clinical sites, enrolling 54 patients to evaluate the treatment's safety and effectiveness.
After receiving Zanvastro for a little more than a year, treated patients demonstrated significantly better walking speeds than patients who had not received the drug.
The results also indicated that treatment could stabilize motor function, an important outcome for a progressive disorder that can steadily undermine a person's ability to move independently. Some participants experienced improvements in motor performance.
These findings helped establish Zanvastro as the first treatment approved to modify the underlying disease process in Alexander disease, rather than focusing exclusively on symptom relief.
The FDA approval covers people with Alexander disease across the full age spectrum, from infancy through adulthood.
Zanvastro is expected to become available in the United States in the weeks following the approval. Outside the United States, access to the drug will be handled through a licensing agreement between Ionis Pharmaceuticals and Recordati, a major pharmaceutical company headquartered in Italy.
A 30-Year Scientific Journey Offers New Hope
For Messing and his colleagues, the approval represents the culmination of more than 30 years of research, beginning with basic investigations into brain cell biology and eventually leading to a treatment for patients.
What started as an unexpected finding in genetically modified mice helped reveal the cause of an extremely rare disease, transformed how doctors diagnose it, and provided the foundation for developing a drug.
The achievement is also an example of translational research, the process of turning discoveries made in laboratories into treatments that can directly benefit patients.
Throughout that journey, individuals living with Alexander disease and their families played an essential role by supporting the research and participating in studies.
"The whole program of research would not have been possible without the support and participation from the patient and family community, to whom we will always be grateful," Messing says.

articles.title: Europe's new Sentinel-3C satellite just sent back spectacular images of Earth
articles.text:
Europe's new Sentinel-3C satellite just sent back spectacular images of Earth
Just two weeks after launch, Europe's Sentinel-3C satellite is revealing stunning views of Earth while preparing to track the dramatic changes transforming our planet.
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- European Space Agency (ESA)
- Summary:
- Europe's Sentinel-3C satellite has returned breathtaking images of Earth just two weeks after launch, revealing the snowy Alps, frozen Arctic islands, and brilliant turquoise Caribbean waters. Its first measurements also show promising results for tracking rising seas, melting ice sheets, and other changes reshaping our planet.
- Share:
Just two weeks after reaching orbit, Europe's new Copernicus Sentinel-3C satellite has delivered its first spectacular images of Earth, revealing everything from the snow-covered Alps to the frozen Arctic and the brilliant turquoise waters of the Caribbean.
But the satellite is doing much more than taking beautiful pictures. Its instruments have also begun measuring ocean heights and the elevation of Greenland's massive ice sheet, providing an early demonstration of technology designed to monitor Earth's changing climate.
The first images and measurements come from two of Sentinel-3C's key instruments. Both are performing well in initial tests, bringing the satellite closer to its mission of tracking environmental changes across the planet.
A Powerful New Satellite to Monitor Earth's Changing Climate
Sentinel-3C is the third spacecraft in Europe's Sentinel-3 satellite series, a central part of the Copernicus Earth observation program. The satellites are equipped with matching sets of instruments that continuously gather information about the oceans, land, atmosphere, and cryosphere, which includes Earth's frozen regions.
Over the oceans, Sentinel-3 measures sea surface temperature, color, and height, along with sea ice thickness. These observations help scientists investigate marine pollution, track marine heatwaves, and understand changes in ocean conditions.
On land, the mission provides valuable information about droughts, wildfires, vegetation health, and how different areas are being used. It also measures water levels in rivers and lakes, as well as changes in the elevation of polar ice sheets.
The data support weather forecasting by providing timely observations of environmental conditions. They also help researchers identify long-term trends linked to climate change.
The European Space Agency (ESA) is still preparing Sentinel-3C for full operation through a detailed testing and commissioning process expected to take another five months. Nevertheless, the satellite's first two weeks in orbit have already produced encouraging results.
Stunning Satellite Images Reveal Italy's Diverse Landscape
One of Sentinel-3C's first images, captured on September 30 by its ocean and land color instrument, offers a remarkable natural-color view of Italy and its surrounding seas.
The image extends from southern Germany across the Italian peninsula to Sicily and the southern Mediterranean. It reveals an extraordinary variety of landscapes, from towering mountains and fertile farmland to deep blue waters.
Near the upper center of the scene, the Po Valley stands out as a broad expanse of green and brown. This fertile region is the heart of Italy's agricultural production. Immediately to the north, the snow-covered Alps rise dramatically above the lowlands, their bright white peaks creating a striking contrast with the surrounding terrain.
Elsewhere across Italy, different shades of green and brown reveal variations in vegetation, farming activity, and land cover.
To the east, the Adriatic Sea separates Italy from the partially visible Balkan Peninsula. Along Italy's eastern coast, bands of lighter blue water stand out against the deeper blue offshore. Scientists believe these color differences are likely caused by sediment carried into the sea by rivers and redistributed by coastal currents.
On the opposite side of the peninsula, the dark waters of the Tyrrhenian Sea surround Sardinia and Sicily. Corsica is also within the image, although clouds obscure much of the island.
Together, the contrasting colors of mountains, farmland, islands, and surrounding seas create a vivid portrait of Italy as seen from space.
A Dramatic View of the Arctic's Vulnerable Ice
Another image captured on September 30 shifts the focus far north to the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, located west of Greenland.
Here, the landscape looks dramatically different. Snow and ice blanket many of the islands, while exposed rock, rugged coastlines, and deep fjords form intricate patterns across the frozen region.
The image was taken near the time of year when Arctic sea ice typically reaches its annual minimum. Much of the surrounding water appears dark and open, although scattered fragments of floating sea ice remain visible.
These observations are particularly important because the Arctic is warming much faster than the global average.
As temperatures rise, glaciers and ice sheets lose mass, while sea ice continues to melt. The disappearance of reflective ice also exposes darker ocean water, which absorbs more solar energy and can accelerate regional warming.
Sentinel-3's different instruments observe ice in complementary ways, helping scientists better understand changes across these vulnerable polar environments.
Brilliant Caribbean Waters Seen From Space
Sentinel-3C's third featured image, captured on September 29, reveals an entirely different side of Earth.
The scene shows part of the Caribbean, with Cuba near the bottom and the Bahamas toward the top. Around the islands, shallow waters glow in brilliant shades of turquoise, contrasting sharply with the dark blue of the deeper surrounding ocean.
These dramatic differences in color help reveal variations in water depth and the characteristics of the marine environment.
The Caribbean image is also a reminder of the challenges facing low-lying islands and coastal communities as global sea levels continue to rise.
One of Sentinel-3C's most important instruments, its synthetic aperture radar altimeter, is designed to measure the height of the ocean surface with high precision. By tracking how that height changes over time, scientists can better understand sea-level rise and support efforts to prepare for its consequences.
New Measurements Show the Satellite Is Performing Well
Beyond its striking photographs, Sentinel-3C has already begun demonstrating its ability to gather precise scientific measurements.
Its radar altimeter has collected sea surface height data across the Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea. Researchers compared these observations with the Copernicus Marine Service's multimission sea-level anomaly data, which combine measurements from multiple satellites.
The early results show good agreement with existing measurements, indicating that the new altimeter is operating as expected.
Once Sentinel-3C completes commissioning, it will contribute to global sea-level monitoring alongside established satellite missions such as Copernicus Sentinel-6 and Jason.
These long-running observations are essential for understanding how quickly the world's oceans are rising.
Thanks to precise satellite measurements, scientists have determined that global sea levels have increased by an average of 3.64 mm per year since 1999. The rate of sea-level rise has also been accelerating, making continued monitoring increasingly important.
Sentinel-3C's altimeter will contribute more than ocean measurements. It will also observe changes in the height of rivers, lakes, sea ice, and land ice, complementing future observations from the upcoming Copernicus CRISTAL mission.
Tracking Greenland's Massive Ice Sheet From Orbit
Some of Sentinel-3C's most encouraging early results come from Greenland.
Between September 30 and October 4, the satellite collected measurements of the Greenland Ice Sheet's surface elevation. An accompanying animation shows the tracks of these observations across the enormous ice-covered landscape.
When scientists compared the measurements with a reference digital elevation model, a detailed representation of the ice sheet's surface, the satellite's observations closely matched the existing data.
This agreement offers further evidence that the radar altimeter is functioning properly.
Accurately tracking ice sheet elevation is particularly important as the planet warms. Greenland and Antarctica contain vast amounts of frozen water, and changes in their ice sheets can have major consequences for global sea levels.
Ice loss from these regions is already a major contributor to sea-level rise. By repeatedly measuring the height of their surfaces, satellites can help scientists monitor changes over time and improve predictions of future sea-level rise.
What's Next for Europe's New Earth-Watching Satellite?
Although Sentinel-3C is still in its early testing phase, its first observations represent an important step toward full scientific operations.
The satellite's ocean and land color instrument has already delivered detailed images of landscapes and coastlines, while its radar altimeter has produced encouraging measurements of ocean and ice sheet elevations.
Another milestone is approaching. The mission is preparing to release the first observations from its sea and land surface temperature radiometer, an instrument designed to measure the temperature of Earth's land and ocean surfaces.
Sentinel-3C is part of Copernicus, the Earth observation component of the European Union's Space Program. ESA is responsible for developing and implementing the Sentinel-3 satellites and operating them through the commissioning period.
After commissioning, ESA and the European Organisation for the Exploitation of Meteorological Satellites (Eumetsat) jointly manage the Sentinel-3 mission.
Eumetsat handles routine satellite operations and supplies marine and atmospheric observations, while ESA provides data covering land, the cryosphere, inland waters, and atmospheric products processed after acquisition.
Together, the two organizations make Sentinel-3 observations available to Copernicus services and users around the world.
With its first images and measurements already demonstrating promising performance, Sentinel-3C is on its way to becoming another important tool for observing Earth's oceans, landscapes, ice sheets, and atmosphere as the planet continues to change.

articles.title: Scientists find a hidden problem with endless smartphone scrolling
articles.text:
Scientists find a hidden problem with endless smartphone scrolling
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- Semmelweis University
- Summary:
- Excessive smartphone use may be taking a hidden toll on the brain and body, with heavy scrolling linked to poorer memory, reduced attention, disrupted sleep, and potential balance problems. Researchers found that weak self-control and fear of missing out, rather than personality alone, are key factors behind problematic phone use.
- Share:
The real problem with smartphone use may not be how many hours people spend staring at their screens. What they do during that time could be even more important.
Researchers at Semmelweis University have found that problematic smartphone use is closely associated with poor self-control and a strong fear of missing out (FOMO), rather than personality traits alone. Their findings also highlight potential consequences for the brain and body. Heavy scrolling is linked to poorer memory, reduced concentration, and disrupted sleep, while prolonged phone use may contribute to posture problems that affect balance and reaction time.
The study, published in Acta Psychologica, suggests that understanding how people interact with their phones could be just as important as monitoring their daily screen time.
What Makes Some People More Vulnerable to Smartphone Addiction?
To investigate the effects of smartphone habits, researchers at Semmelweis University studied students between the ages of 18 and 35, examining their phone use alongside measures of mental health, physical health, and cognitive performance.
Participants completed online questionnaires about their daily smartphone activities, including how much time they spent actively using their devices and what they typically did on them. They were also asked whether using their phones had caused them to miss planned activities and whether they continued thinking about their phones even when they were not using them.
The researchers then examined several psychological factors that might influence problematic smartphone use. These included self-control, fear of missing out on social experiences, and neuroticism, a personality trait associated with a greater tendency to experience negative emotions such as anxiety, sadness, fear, and anger.
By analyzing these responses, the team identified three distinct patterns of smartphone use.
People in the "pure social" group primarily used their phones to communicate with friends, maintain relationships, and interact with others. Those classified as "light process" users spent less than four to five hours a day using their phones for a mixture of social interaction, news, entertainment, and passive scrolling.
The third group, known as "heavy process" users, accounted for approximately one third of participants. These individuals spent four to five hours or more on their phones each day, largely consuming online content rather than communicating directly with other people.
The differences between these groups helped researchers identify the factors most strongly associated with problematic phone habits.
"Our main finding is that personality alone -- such as a high level of neuroticism -- does not make someone addicted to their phone. People who are more prone to negative emotions like anxiety, depression, or stress do not automatically become addicted. What really matters is how well they can control their behavior, emotions, and impulses, and how strongly they fear missing out," said Dr. Johanna Takács, senior research fellow at the Faculty of Health Sciences at Semmelweis University and lead researcher of the study.
Why Endless Smartphone Scrolling May Be Worse Than Screen Time Alone
One of the most important findings was that the type of smartphone activity mattered, particularly when it came to attention, memory, and other aspects of mental performance.
Passively scrolling through social media feeds or watching one short video after another exposes users to a rapid stream of changing information. The researchers suggest that this constant stimulation can strain attention, make sustained concentration more difficult, and contribute to mental fatigue.
Cognitive testing revealed that participants in the heavy process group performed worse on memory and attention tasks than would be expected for their age. They also reported poorer sleep, a stronger desire for continuous stimulation, and greater difficulty resisting the urge to immediately check their phones or act on impulses.
These findings suggest that spending hours consuming content may be associated with different mental outcomes than using a phone primarily to communicate with others. However, the results do not establish that scrolling directly causes the observed differences in cognitive performance.
How Smartphone Use Can Affect Posture and Balance
Although the way people used their phones appeared especially important for cognitive performance, total usage time was more closely associated with physical consequences.
One concern is the posture people adopt while looking at their screens. Holding a smartphone below eye level often causes the head to tilt forward, placing additional pressure on the neck and surrounding structures.
Over time, this position can contribute to what is commonly called text neck, a posture problem that may have consequences beyond neck discomfort.
"When people hold their phones at waist or chest level and look down at them, the head moves forward, creating a forward head posture, also known as "text neck." This puts extra strain on the neck and can cause pain or early wear and tear of the neck joints. The neck contains receptors that tell the brain how the head is positioned. If a forward head posture is maintained for long periods, these signals can change and lead to balance problems. These effects are not limited to phone use but can also influence everyday movements," said Beáta Seregély, assistant lecturer and expert responsible for the physical measurements in the study.
These effects may occur because the neck plays an important role in helping the brain understand the position and movement of the head. When prolonged forward head posture changes the information coming from these sensory receptors, it may interfere with balance and coordination during everyday activities.
The researchers also highlighted potential effects on reaction time and concentration, suggesting that excessive phone use could have consequences extending beyond the moments spent looking at a screen.
Simple Ways to Reduce the Risks of Smartphone Overuse
Despite these concerns, the researchers do not believe that eliminating smartphones from young people's lives is the answer. Instead, they recommend developing healthier habits and becoming more aware of how and why phones are used.
Practical strategies include reducing unnecessary notifications, particularly from social media and messaging applications, and setting limits on time spent browsing social platforms. Avoiding smartphone use before bedtime may also help protect sleep, while regular physical activity and better posture could reduce some of the physical strain associated with prolonged use.
The psychological side of smartphone use may be equally important.
Because weak self-control and fear of missing out were strongly associated with problematic use, the researchers emphasize helping young people manage impulses and feel less pressure to stay constantly connected. Behavioral training and psychological support could help strengthen these skills.
The findings suggest that even people who are naturally more anxious, emotionally sensitive, or vulnerable to stress are not necessarily destined to develop unhealthy smartphone habits. Better self-control and less fear of missing out may substantially reduce that vulnerability.
Ultimately, the research points to an important distinction. Reducing screen time can be helpful, but changing how people use their smartphones may be just as important for protecting attention, sleep, and overall well-being.

articles.title: Your gut bacteria could be changing how many calories you absorb
articles.text:
Your gut bacteria could be changing how many calories you absorb
The calories printed on food labels may not reflect how much energy your body actually absorbs.
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- Arizona State University
- Summary:
- Scientists have developed a model showing that gut bacteria play a surprisingly important role in how many calories we absorb, meaning food labels may not tell the full story. In a controlled study, people eating a high-fiber diet absorbed about 116 fewer calories per day than those eating a typical Western diet, without feeling hungrier.
- Share:
The calorie count printed on a food package might seem like a straightforward measure of how much energy you will get from eating it. But the number on the label does not necessarily match the calories your body actually absorbs. One reason is that digestion involves more than just breaking down food. It also depends on trillions of microorganisms living inside your digestive system.
Researchers at Arizona State University have developed a mathematical model that explores this often overlooked part of digestion. Known as DAMM, short for digestion, absorption and microbial metabolism, the model tracks how food moves through the digestive tract, how much energy the body absorbs directly, and how gut microbes process whatever remains. It also estimates which products of digestion are absorbed and which leave the body as waste.
By accounting for the relationship between diet, human digestion, and gut bacteria, the researchers hope to improve our understanding of obesity, diabetes, and other metabolic disorders. With further development, the approach could eventually help health care professionals create diets tailored to individual patients.
"Digestion is not just a human process -- it is a collaboration between our bodies and trillions of microbes living in the gut," said Professor Rosa Krajmalnik-Brown. "DAMM gives us a powerful new way to quantify how those microbial partners contribute to human health and energy balance, and also point at the importance of properly feeding our gut microbes."
Krajmalnik-Brown is director of ASU's Biodesign Center for Health Through Microbiomes and a professor in the university's School of Sustainable Engineering and the Built Environment.
The research team also included ASU Professor Bruce Rittmann, director of the Biodesign Swette Center for Environmental Biotechnology and a Regents Professor of environmental engineering, along with first author Taylor Davis, an ASU graduate research assistant. Scientists at the AdventHealth Translational Research Institute in Orlando, Florida, collaborated on the project.
The findings were published in PLOS One.
Why Traditional Calorie Counts Miss Part of the Picture
For more than 100 years, scientists have used a system based on Atwater parameters to estimate how much energy people can obtain from food. This method assigns average calorie values to each gram of fat, carbohydrates, and protein, then uses those values to calculate the total available energy.
Although this approach is practical and widely used, it cannot fully explain what happens during digestion. In particular, it does not account for how different foods nourish gut bacteria or how those bacteria transform undigested material into substances the body can use for energy.
One important example involves short-chain fatty acids. These compounds are produced when microbes in the colon break down fiber and other food components that pass through the upper digestive tract without being absorbed. Some of these fatty acids can enter the bloodstream and provide additional calories.
To better understand these interactions, the researchers built on an earlier controlled diet study investigating how the gut microbiome influences human energy balance. The gut microbiome consists of the enormous community of bacteria and other microorganisms that inhabit the digestive system.
A High-Fiber Diet Led to 116 Fewer Calories Absorbed Per Day
In the clinical study, healthy adults followed one of two carefully designed eating plans. The first was a microbiome-enhancer diet containing substantial amounts of fiber and resistant starch (less processed foods and foods with larger particle size). Resistant starch is a type of carbohydrate that escapes much of the usual digestion in the small intestine, allowing it to reach the colon, where microbes can break it down.
The second eating plan resembled a typical Western diet, with lower amounts of fiber and resistant starch (more processed foods and smaller particle size).
Despite both diets being designed for the study, participants absorbed noticeably different amounts of energy. Those consuming the Western diet absorbed approximately 116 more calories per day than those eating the fiber-rich diet.
Perhaps just as interesting, the people following the higher-fiber eating plan did not report feeling hungrier.
The findings suggest that the amount of energy people obtain from food depends partly on its composition and how it moves through the digestive system. Differences in food processing, fiber content, and microbial activity can all influence the final outcome.
"What is truly unique about the DAMM model is that it quantitatively links human metabolism to the metabolism of the microorganisms in the colon in a way that matches the results from the clinical study and provides fundamental insight into how the microbial community works in partnership with the human host," Rittmann said.
Gut Bacteria Can Supply About 140 Calories a Day
The DAMM model offers a more detailed way to follow the energy contained in food from the moment it enters the digestive system.
First, it examines the protein, carbohydrate, and fat content of a person's diet and estimates how much usable energy is absorbed in the upper gastrointestinal tract.
It then tracks the remaining material as it moves into the colon. Here, gut microbes break down nutrients that escaped earlier digestion, producing compounds such as short-chain fatty acids. The body can absorb some of these compounds through the colon and use them as another source of energy.
The model also includes methane production by certain microorganisms called methanogens, which generate methane as part of their metabolism.
According to the researchers' calculations, short-chain fatty acids absorbed from the colon supplied an average of approximately 140 calories per day. That represents about 7.4% of the total usable energy obtained from food.
More broadly, the model estimated that roughly 85% of usable energy came from the upper gastrointestinal tract, while approximately 15% came from the lower gastrointestinal tract, where microbes are especially important.
These findings highlight why traditional calorie calculations cannot fully describe human digestion. A meaningful share of the energy available to the body is influenced by microbial processes that conventional food-label calculations do not explicitly measure.
When the team compared DAMM's predictions with actual measurements from the controlled diet study, the model produced estimates that were closer to the observed calorie absorption than those generated using the conventional Atwater approach.
The older method generally underestimated how many calories participants absorbed. By including microbial metabolism, DAMM provided a more accurate estimate of the energy obtained from the different diets.
How Fiber Changes the Calorie Equation
One of the model's most revealing features is its ability to account for differences between diets.
The microbiome-enhancer diet delivered more fiber and other fermentable material to the colon. This gave gut microbes additional substances to break down, increasing their production of short-chain fatty acids.
DAMM predicted this increase, consistent with the pattern observed in the controlled clinical trial. Participants consuming the microbiome-enhancer diet had higher levels of short-chain fatty acids in measurements taken from their blood serum and feces.
These compounds are important because they illustrate how closely microbial activity and human metabolism are connected. Gut bacteria can transform food components that would otherwise pass through the digestive system into molecules that the body can absorb and use for energy.
However, producing more of these compounds does not necessarily mean absorbing more calories overall.
In fact, participants following the microbiome-enhancer diet absorbed fewer net calories than those eating the Western diet, even though the higher-fiber diet supported greater microbial activity and increased short-chain fatty acid production.
This apparent contradiction becomes easier to understand when the different stages of digestion are examined separately. Although gut microbes can generate additional usable energy, the amount absorbed directly from food in the upper digestive tract also matters.
DAMM helps researchers distinguish between these contributions. It estimates how much energy the body extracts before food reaches the colon, how much energy microbes produce from the remaining material, and how much ultimately gets absorbed or eliminated.
Toward More Personalized Diets and Better Nutrition
By bringing human digestion and microbial metabolism into a single mathematical framework, the researchers have created a tool that could help explain why different diets produce different effects on the body's energy balance.
The approach may eventually improve scientists' understanding of how diet influences obesity, diabetes, and other metabolic conditions. It also raises the possibility of designing nutrition plans that consider not only the nutrients in food but also how those nutrients interact with the microbes living inside each person's gut.
For now, the model provides a research framework rather than a ready-to-use method for prescribing personalized diets. Further studies will be needed to determine how well it performs across different populations, eating patterns, and microbiome compositions.
The researchers also expect the model to become more sophisticated as scientists uncover additional details about how microorganisms and the human body exchange nutrients and energy.
"The DAMM model is more than just a tool for characterizing diet," Davis said. "It's a framework designed to evolve. As we discover more on how diet, metabolism and the microbes interact, the new insights can be incorporated into the model, allowing it to grow with us as we learn."

articles.title: Scientists uncover the 2.3-billion-year-old secret that helped keep Earth habitable
articles.text:
Scientists uncover the 2.3-billion-year-old secret that helped keep Earth habitable
Researchers may have solved a 2.3-billion-year-old mystery about how Earth's oceans helped keep the planet oxygen-rich and habitable.
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Riverside
- Summary:
- Scientists may have solved a 2.3-billion-year-old mystery about how Earth maintained enough oxygen to support life. Ancient rocks reveal that phosphorus recycling in the oceans created a self-sustaining cycle that helped keep oxygen levels high, even as the planet underwent dramatic environmental changes. The discovery challenges assumptions about Earth's early atmosphere and raises new questions about why complex life took so long to emerge.
- Share:
More than 2 billion years ago, Earth underwent a dramatic transformation as oxygen began building up in its atmosphere. But that change left scientists with a major mystery: How did the planet maintain enough oxygen to remain habitable over millions of years?
Researchers have now uncovered evidence that the answer may lie in an ancient recycling system within Earth's oceans. By studying rocks from South Africa, they found that changes in ocean chemistry helped create a natural cycle in which biological activity supported the continued accumulation of atmospheric oxygen.
The research, published in Nature Communications, involved scientists including University of California, Riverside geologist Andrey Bekker. Their findings suggest that phosphorus, a nutrient essential for life, played a central role in sustaining the oxygen levels that would eventually help make more complex organisms possible.
How Ancient Oceans Helped Sustain Earth's Oxygen
About 2.3 billion years ago, Earth experienced the Great Oxidation Event, a major turning point when oxygen became a lasting component of the atmosphere. Scientists have understood this transition for decades, but explaining how oxygen remained sufficiently abundant afterward has been much more difficult.
The researchers identified a feedback loop that may help explain what happened. As oxygen spread into the oceans, it altered the chemistry of seawater and increased concentrations of sulfate, a compound containing sulfur and oxygen.
Certain microbes used this sulfate to break down organic material more efficiently. In the process, they released phosphorus back into the water, making this vital nutrient available to other organisms.
With more phosphorus available, biological productivity increased. That meant more organic carbon could eventually become buried in seafloor sediments rather than being broken down. Because the decomposition of organic matter can consume oxygen, burying more carbon helped favor the continued buildup of oxygen in the atmosphere.
This created a reinforcing cycle in which rising oxygen levels encouraged chemical changes that supported biological growth, which in turn helped maintain atmospheric oxygen.
"Living things cannot grow or function properly without phosphorus," Bekker said. "Once more of it became available in the oceans, it allowed more organic carbon to be buried. A side effect of that process is that more oxygen continued to be released into the atmosphere."
Ancient Rocks Reveal a Hidden Phosphorus Cycle
To investigate this process, the scientists examined ancient rock samples from South Africa using a technique that provides a more detailed picture of phosphorus availability in prehistoric oceans.
Earlier research could determine how much phosphorus was present in ancient rocks, but those measurements revealed little about whether organisms could actually use it. Some phosphorus becomes trapped in minerals, making it effectively inaccessible to living things.
The researchers addressed this limitation by separating phosphorus according to the minerals that contained it. They accomplished this by dissolving different mineral components one at a time, allowing them to distinguish phosphorus that had been available for biological activity from phosphorus locked away in mineral structures.
This distinction is crucial because the total amount of phosphorus in an ocean does not necessarily indicate how much is available to sustain life. The new approach provides a clearer way to reconstruct ancient nutrient cycles and understand how they influenced atmospheric oxygen.
"We can now separate the phosphorus that was available to organisms from phosphorus that was essentially locked away," Bekker said. "That gives us a much clearer picture of nutrient levels in ancient oceans than we had before."
Earth's Oxygen History May Have Been More Turbulent Than Expected
The findings also point to a more complicated history of Earth's atmosphere than scientists previously recognized.
Rather than remaining relatively steady after the Great Oxidation Event, oxygen levels may have risen and fallen much more dramatically. These fluctuations likely continued to influence ocean chemistry and the movement of essential nutrients through marine environments over tens of millions of years.
The results could also change how scientists interpret the evolution of early life.
One longstanding question is why complex organisms took so long to appear after oxygen first became a significant part of Earth's atmosphere. Limited oxygen has often been considered a possible explanation for this delay.
However, if oxygen remained relatively abundant during extended periods of Earth's early history, it raises the possibility that other environmental conditions or biological limitations played a greater role in slowing the emergence of complex life.
What Earth's Ancient Oxygen Cycle Means for the Future
Although the research focuses on events billions of years in the past, its implications extend to the oceans we depend on today.
Climate change is already contributing to declining oxygen levels in parts of the world's oceans. If oxygen loss continues, it could disrupt phosphorus recycling and reduce the amount of this essential nutrient available to marine organisms.
Such changes could limit biological productivity and make ocean ecosystems less resilient to environmental stress.
The findings may also help scientists search for signs of life beyond Earth. Worlds with oceans are considered promising places to investigate potential habitability, but the presence of water alone does not guarantee that conditions can support life over long periods.
Understanding how oxygen, nutrients, and biological processes interacted throughout Earth's history could help researchers identify similar chemical relationships on distant planets and other ocean-bearing worlds.
"Earth's history shows that oxygen, nutrients, and life evolved together," Bekker said. "Understanding those connections gives us a more nuanced perspective on our own planet's future and what we might look for on other planets."

articles.title: Scientists find a surprising genetic twist behind octopus intelligence
articles.text:
Scientists find a surprising genetic twist behind octopus intelligence
Researchers uncovered an ancient DNA reshuffling that may help explain how octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish evolved their extraordinary intelligence.
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- University of Vienna
- Summary:
- The remarkable intelligence of octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish may trace back to an ancient reshuffling of their DNA that created new connections between genes. Scientists discovered that these changes in the genome's 3D structure may have helped drive the evolution of their unusually complex nervous systems.
- Share:
Octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish possess some of the most sophisticated nervous systems in the animal kingdom, giving them remarkable abilities such as solving problems and rapidly changing their appearance to blend into their surroundings. But how did these extraordinary capabilities evolve? Scientists have uncovered a surprising clue that may lie not in the genes themselves, but in the way DNA is folded and arranged inside cells.
Researchers at the University of Vienna discovered that a massive reorganization of DNA hundreds of millions of years ago brought previously separated genetic regions into contact. These newly formed connections changed how genes could interact and be controlled, potentially helping drive the evolution of the unusually complex nervous systems found in these animals, which are collectively known as coleoid cephalopods.
The findings, published in Nature Communications, suggest that the physical structure of DNA may play a much more active role in evolution than scientists once thought.
How the 3D Structure of DNA Influences Evolution
To investigate this possibility, the research team reconstructed the three-dimensional organization of the genome in octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish. They then compared the arrangement of DNA with patterns of gene activity to understand how changes in genome structure might influence biological complexity.
"The genome isn't just a sequence of genes. It's folded into a complex three-dimensional structure," said lead author Dr. Thea Rogers. "Understanding how that structure evolves is becoming increasingly important for understanding how new forms of biological complexity arise."
Although DNA is often pictured as a long, twisted ladder, it does not simply stretch out inside a cell. Instead, it folds into an intricate three-dimensional arrangement, allowing sections that are far apart along the DNA sequence to come into close physical contact.
These connections matter because they can influence which genes are activated, when they are used, and how strongly they function. Changes in the way DNA folds can therefore alter gene activity without necessarily changing the underlying genetic instructions.
An Ancient DNA Reshuffling Created New Genetic Connections
The researchers found evidence that cephalopod genomes underwent an extensive period of reorganization hundreds of millions of years ago. During this evolutionary upheaval, large sections of genetic material were rearranged, bringing regions of chromosomes that had previously been separated into close proximity.
This reshuffling created opportunities for DNA regions to interact in ways that had not previously been possible. Once these connections formed, they could influence each other's activity, gradually establishing more elaborate networks of genetic regulation.
Over evolutionary time, the interactions could become increasingly interconnected and difficult to separate, creating a process the scientists describe as "regulatory entanglement."
This mechanism offers a possible explanation for how evolution can produce new biological features without disrupting the essential functions organisms need to survive. By establishing new connections among existing genetic elements, the genome may develop different patterns of gene activity while keeping crucial biological systems intact.
Stable DNA Structures and Flexible Genetic Loops
One of the study's most revealing findings was that different parts of the genome responded very differently to evolutionary reorganization.
The researchers discovered that large structural regions called chromatin domains remained remarkably stable over long periods of evolutionary history. These domains help organize DNA into broad sections within the cell, and their persistence suggests that some features of genome architecture are strongly conserved.
Smaller structures known as chromatin loops, however, told a different story.
These loops form when distant sections of DNA are brought together in three-dimensional space. Unlike the relatively stable chromatin domains, the loops showed substantial differences between cephalopod species, between tissues, and across stages of development.
Particularly intriguing was their location. Many of these flexible DNA connections appeared near genes associated with important cephalopod characteristics, including the development and function of the nervous system.
This pattern suggests that smaller, more adaptable structures within the genome may be especially responsive to major genetic rearrangements. By changing which regions of DNA can communicate, these flexible connections could help generate new patterns of gene activity and contribute to the evolution of complex traits.
A New Clue to the Evolution of Octopus Intelligence
The discovery challenges a traditional view of genome architecture as something that primarily changes in response to evolution. Instead, the findings suggest that the physical organization of DNA can itself influence how evolutionary changes unfold.
In octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish, ancient rearrangements of the genome may have helped establish new regulatory networks that contributed to the development of their exceptionally sophisticated nervous systems.
The results do not establish that these DNA changes directly caused the evolution of cephalopod intelligence. However, they reveal a potential mechanism through which large genetic rearrangements could create new biological possibilities while preserving essential functions.
More broadly, the research points to an often overlooked dimension of evolution. The emergence of extraordinary traits may depend not only on which genes an organism inherits, but also on how those genes are physically arranged and connected within the cell.

articles.title: Popular weight loss drugs linked to a surprising fingernail problem
articles.text:
Popular weight loss drugs linked to a surprising fingernail problem
Scientists have uncovered a surprising link between popular GLP-1 weight loss drugs and nail detachment, hair loss, and scalp inflammation.
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- Beyond
- Summary:
- Popular GLP-1 weight loss drugs, such as Ozempic and Wegovy, have been linked to unexpectedly high rates of nail detachment, hair loss, and scalp inflammation, with some problems occurring several times more frequently among users. Researchers found that weight loss alone could not fully explain the differences, suggesting there may be more to these overlooked symptoms.
- Share:
Popular GLP-1 medications used for weight loss and type 2 diabetes (such as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound, Victoza, and Trulicity) have been linked to an unexpected problem involving fingernails. A multinational study found that people taking these drugs were more than four times as likely to report nail detachment, a condition in which the nail separates from the skin underneath it.
Researchers found that 39% of GLP-1 users experienced nail detachment, compared with just 9% of people who had never taken the medications. Nail discoloration was also considerably more common, and two-thirds (66%) of users reported at least one nail disorder.
The findings, presented at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) Congress 2026, come from the first controlled study to investigate the possible relationship between GLP-1 medications and nail health.
Unexpected Nail Problems Among GLP-1 Users
GLP-1 receptor agonists have become increasingly popular for managing obesity and type 2 diabetes. These medications act on a hormone signaling system that helps regulate blood sugar and appetite, making them effective tools for improving metabolic health and supporting weight loss.
However, scientists are still investigating their potential effects on other parts of the body. Until recently, information about nail changes during GLP-1 treatment came primarily from individual reports of possible adverse reactions, rather than controlled comparisons.
To investigate the connection, researchers examined 575 people using GLP-1 medications and compared them with 1,329 individuals who had type 2 diabetes and/or obesity but had never used the drugs. Participants were recruited from France, the United States, Brazil, and Mexico.
The results revealed a consistent pattern. Overall, 66% of GLP-1 users reported at least one nail disorder, compared with 53% of the control group. Nail discoloration showed an especially large difference, affecting 46% of users versus 17% of nonusers.
Nail detachment was even more striking, with reports more than four times as common among those taking GLP-1 medications.
Weight Loss Alone May Not Explain the Nail Changes
One important question was whether the nail problems might simply be related to weight loss, rather than to the medications themselves. Rapid changes in body weight can affect nutrition and other physiological processes, potentially influencing nail and hair health.
However, the researchers found that weight loss did not fully account for the differences. Even when they limited their analysis to participants who had lost weight, GLP-1 users continued to report significantly more nail problems than those who had not used the medications.
"Until now, nail changes associated with GLP-1 therapies had essentially been anecdotal," said study author Dr. Charles Taïeb. "Our findings show a clear association, but they also underline an important point: not everything that happens during GLP-1 treatment is necessarily caused by the treatment itself."
The researchers emphasized that their findings do not prove that GLP-1 drugs cause nail disorders. Approximately half of the medication users said they had experienced nail problems even before beginning treatment.
When the researchers accounted for existing skin conditions and nutritional deficiencies, some of the differences between the groups became smaller. Nevertheless, nail detachment and discoloration remained approximately two to three times more common among GLP-1 users after these adjustments.
Scientists Also Find Higher Rates of Hair Loss and Scalp Problems
The unexpected findings were not limited to fingernails.
A companion study examining the same participants identified significant differences in hair and scalp health among people taking GLP-1 medications.
Half of GLP-1 users reported unusual hair loss, compared with 34% of nonusers. Reduced hair volume or density was also substantially more common, affecting 42% of users versus 19% of the control group.
Researchers additionally examined hair loss that began after treatment started. This was reported by 26% of GLP-1 users, compared with 12% of nonusers, making it more than twice as common in the medication group.
Scalp redness was approximately three times more frequent among GLP-1 users.
A particularly interesting finding was that hair loss rarely appeared by itself. Most users who reported shedding also experienced other scalp symptoms, including itching, redness or flaking skin.
These accompanying symptoms raised the possibility that inflammation could be contributing to the changes, rather than the hair loss being explained entirely by rapid weight reduction.
"This suggests that what is happening on the scalp may go beyond the classical shedding seen after rapid weight loss and involve an inflammatory component," explained study author Dr. Bruno Halioua. "Scalp inflammation was the rule rather than the exception, which clinicians do not currently look for and which may be treatable. Taken together, our findings suggest that factors beyond weight loss alone may contribute to the hair, scalp and nail changes observed among GLP-1 users."
What the Findings Mean for People Taking GLP-1 Drugs
Despite the relatively high frequency of reported symptoms, the researchers stressed that the findings should encourage awareness rather than alarm.
"These changes are frequent, usually benign, and are not a reason to stop an effective treatment on one's own initiative," he said. "Anyone who notices hair shedding, an itchy or red scalp or nail changes should mention it to their doctor rather than discontinue therapy."
There are also important limitations to consider. Both investigations were cross-sectional studies, meaning they examined participants' experiences without following them over time to establish how symptoms developed. The findings also relied on symptoms reported by participants rather than standardized clinical examinations.
As a result, the studies can reveal patterns and associations, but they cannot determine whether GLP-1 medications directly caused the reported nail, hair, or scalp problems.
To investigate these questions more thoroughly, the research team plans to conduct prospective studies that follow patients from the beginning of treatment. These investigations will include standardized skin, hair and nail examinations along with biological monitoring.
The goal is to establish when the changes first appear, identify the mechanisms behind them, and determine whether they improve or disappear over time.
The research received institutional support from DUCRAY Laboratories (Pierre Fabre Group), a company specializing in dermatological and hair care products developed to help manage skin and scalp conditions and improve quality of life.

articles.title: Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice
articles.text:
Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- PLOS
- Summary:
- Scientists discovered that declining levels of a protein called Menin may help drive aging, and restoring it in older mice reversed several age-related changes in just 30 days. Even more surprisingly, supplementing with a simple amino acid called D-serine improved memory and learning, offering a potential new approach to age-related cognitive decline.
- Share:
What if some of the changes we associate with aging begin with the loss of a single protein deep inside the brain? Scientists investigating that possibility found that restoring a protein called Menin in older mice improved memory, balance, bone mass, and skin thickness in just 30 days. Even more surprisingly, supplementing the animals with a naturally occurring amino acid improved their learning and memory in only three weeks.
The findings, originally published in March 2023 in PLOS Biology, came from researchers led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in China. Their experiments identified a previously overlooked connection between inflammation, brain chemistry, and aging throughout the body. Although the results were obtained in mice, they raised an intriguing possibility: Some effects of aging may be influenced by biological processes in the brain that scientists could eventually learn to modify.
Research published since then has added evidence that the brain plays an important role in regulating aging. It has also revealed why the seemingly simple supplement findings deserve careful interpretation.
How a Hidden Brain Protein May Influence Aging
At the center of the discovery is the hypothalamus, a small but powerful region near the base of the brain. It helps regulate essential functions such as body temperature, hunger, metabolism, sleep, and hormone production. Because these systems affect nearly every organ, changes in the hypothalamus can have consequences throughout the body.
Scientists have increasingly recognized the hypothalamus as an important player in aging. One possible reason involves neuroinflammation, the brain's inflammatory response. Although inflammation helps protect against infections and injuries, persistent inflammation can interfere with normal cellular function and contribute to age-related deterioration.
Earlier work by Leng and colleagues had identified Menin as a protein that helps restrain inflammation in the hypothalamus. Menin also participates in regulating gene activity, allowing it to influence multiple biological pathways.
The researchers wanted to understand what happens when this protective protein begins to disappear with age.
They discovered that Menin levels gradually declined in certain hypothalamic neurons as mice grew older. Interestingly, the same decrease was not observed in astrocytes or microglia, two other important types of brain cells involved in supporting neurons and managing immune responses.
To investigate whether this decline actually contributed to aging, the team developed genetically modified mice in which Menin could be selectively disabled.
The results were striking. Mice with reduced Menin activity developed greater inflammation in the hypothalamus, thinner skin, reduced bone mass, and worsening cognitive performance. Their lifespans were also modestly shortened.
Rather than simply accompanying aging, the loss of Menin appeared capable of helping drive several of its characteristic changes.
Restoring Menin Reversed Several Signs of Aging in 30 Days
The researchers then asked an even more interesting question: If declining Menin contributes to aging, could restoring the protein reverse some of the damage?
To find out, they used a gene delivery technique to increase Menin production in a specific part of the hypothalamus in older (20-month-old) mice. This region, called the ventromedial hypothalamus, helps coordinate metabolism, energy balance, and other bodily functions.
Just 30 days after treatment, the animals showed measurable improvements.
Their skin became thicker, bone mass increased, and performance improved on tests measuring learning, memory, and balance. Researchers also observed reductions in inflammation and improvements in certain metabolic changes associated with aging.
In a separate survival analysis, mice receiving the Menin treatment also lived longer than untreated controls.
These findings suggested that some biological changes associated with old age could be at least partially reversed by restoring Menin activity in a specific group of brain cells.
But the researchers also uncovered an important clue about how Menin produced these effects.
A Simple Amino Acid Offers a Surprising Clue
When Menin levels declined, the researchers noticed that concentrations of D-serine, an amino acid involved in brain signaling, also fell.
Amino acids are best known as the building blocks of proteins, but some perform other important functions. D-serine helps regulate NMDA receptors, specialized proteins on nerve cells that are essential for communication between neurons, learning, and the formation of memories.
D-serine is closely related to L-serine, an amino acid commonly found in foods such as soybeans, eggs, fish, and nuts. The two forms have different biological roles. Although D-serine is also available as a dietary supplement, consuming ordinary serine-rich foods is not equivalent to taking the form used in the experiments.
Further investigation revealed that Menin helps control the production of PHGDH, an enzyme involved in the biochemical pathway that generates serine (which was in turn regulated by Menin). When Menin activity decreased, this pathway became less active, reducing the amount of D-serine available to the brain.
Restoring Menin increased D-serine levels in the hippocampus, a region especially important for learning and memory.
This connection suggested that the cognitive effects of declining Menin might be partly explained by disruptions in D-serine signaling.
To test the idea directly, the scientists gave older mice D-serine in their drinking water for three weeks.
The supplementation improved their performance on learning and memory tests, even without directly restoring Menin.
However, there was an important distinction. While increasing Menin improved both cognitive function and physical signs of aging, D-serine supplementation primarily improved cognition. It did not restore the age-related losses in bone mass and skin thickness.
That difference suggests Menin influences aging through several biological mechanisms, with D-serine accounting for only part of its effects.
Later Research Strengthens the Link Between the Brain and Aging
Since the original 2023 discovery, additional studies have provided evidence that the hypothalamus helps coordinate aging across the body.
In a 2024 study published in Cell Metabolism, researchers at Washington University School of Medicine identified a different group of hypothalamic neurons that communicates with fat tissue. By maintaining or stimulating this communication pathway, they increased physical activity, improved age-related metabolic function, and extended lifespan in mice.
That work involved a different protein and neural circuit from Menin, but supported the broader idea that signals originating in the hypothalamus can influence how the rest of the body ages.
Another 2024 study in the Journal of Physiology and Biochemistry provided additional insight into Menin itself. Researchers found that increasing Menin helped protect cultured hippocampal cells against inflammation and a form of programmed cell death triggered by exposure to the stress hormone corticosterone. Although these laboratory experiments did not establish an anti-aging effect, they supported the idea that Menin has important protective functions in brain cells.
An even larger picture emerged in January 2025, when scientists published a detailed analysis of approximately 1.2 million mouse brain cells in Nature.
The researchers discovered that some of the brain cells most sensitive to aging were concentrated around the third ventricle, a fluid-filled cavity in the hypothalamus. Many aging cells showed reduced activity in genes involved in normal neuronal function and increased activity in genes associated with inflammation and immune responses.
These findings highlighted the hypothalamus as a potential center of vulnerability during brain aging, although they did not directly test the Menin pathway.
New Findings in 2026 Reveal More Aging Pathways
Research published in 2026 has further strengthened the connection between hypothalamic activity and longevity.
In a study published in Cell, scientists found that strengthening daily biological rhythms in a specific hypothalamic region improved several aging-related measurements and extended lifespan in male mice. The intervention also reduced estimates of biological age based on DNA methylation, chemical modifications to DNA that change with age.
Another 2026 study in Cell Metabolism identified a protein called Mimecan that helps skeletal muscles communicate with the hypothalamus and brown fat, a specialized tissue involved in generating body heat. Restoring circulating Mimecan levels in older mice improved this communication and extended lifespan.
Together, these discoveries suggest that aging involves complex communication between the brain and the rest of the body. Rather than depending on one master switch, multiple neural circuits, hormones, and metabolic signals appear to help determine how age-related changes unfold.
Could D-Serine Supplements Protect the Human Brain?
The possibility of improving memory with a relatively simple amino acid is especially appealing. However, evidence that D-serine can reverse age-related cognitive decline in humans remains limited.
A small randomized clinical trial published in 2016 tested D-serine in 50 healthy older adults. Participants performed better on one assessment of spatial learning and problem-solving after receiving the amino acid, but researchers did not find significant improvements across the other cognitive tests or mood measurements.
More importantly, later research suggests that the effects of D-serine depend on the biological circumstances.
In an April 2025 study published in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences, scientists investigated D-serine in mice genetically engineered to develop features of Alzheimer's disease.
Unlike the Menin experiments, which associated reduced D-serine with age-related memory impairment, this study found that an early increase in D-serine accompanied disruptions in brain signaling. Removing the enzyme responsible for producing D-serine prevented or reduced several later cognitive impairments in those mice.
These findings do not invalidate the earlier results. Instead, they suggest that D-serine signaling is more complicated than simply having too little or too much. Its effects may depend on the condition being studied, the timing of treatment, and how the brain's signaling systems are functioning.
There are also unanswered questions about the long-term safety of D-serine supplementation. High doses have raised kidney safety concerns in animal experiments, and research has not established whether prolonged supplementation is a safe or effective way to prevent age-related memory loss in otherwise healthy people.
For now, D-serine should be considered an experimental approach rather than a proven treatment for brain aging.
Can Scientists Eventually Slow Aging by Targeting the Brain?
Despite the encouraging mouse experiments, researchers still need to answer several fundamental questions.
Why does Menin decline in the hypothalamus as animals age? How many of its effects could be reversed by treatment, and how long would those improvements last? Could restoring Menin influence other biological systems in unexpected ways?
It is also unclear whether treatments targeting Menin or D-serine could reproduce similar results in humans.
Nevertheless, the original researchers believe the pathway deserves further investigation.
"We speculate that the decline of Menin expression in the hypothalamus with age may be one of the driving factors of aging, and Menin may be the key protein connecting the genetic, inflammatory, and metabolic factors of aging. D-serine is a potentially promising therapeutic for cognitive decline," said Leng.
Leng adds, "Ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) Menin signaling diminished in aged mice, which contributes to systemic aging phenotypes and cognitive deficits. The effects of Menin on aging are mediated by neuroinflammatory changes and metabolic pathway signaling, accompanied by serine deficiency in VMH, while restoration of Menin in VMH reversed aging-related phenotypes."
The growing body of evidence points toward a potentially important shift in how scientists understand aging. Instead of viewing it only as the gradual deterioration of individual organs, researchers are investigating how specific brain pathways may actively shape the process.
The possibility that restoring those pathways could improve memory, physical function, or longevity remains experimental. But the Menin discovery, together with subsequent findings, offers a compelling reason to explore whether some of the biological changes associated with aging are more reversible than previously thought.

articles.title: NASA captures a stunning transformation in Australia's red outback
articles.text:
NASA captures a stunning transformation in Australia's red outback
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- NASA Earth Observatory
- Summary:
- Australia's normally dry, rust-colored outback has erupted into a spectacular carpet of wildflowers after unusually heavy rains, potentially producing its most impressive bloom in nearly 20 years. NASA satellite images capture the stunning transformation, which has even brought rare flowers to the grounds of a remote deep-space observatory.
- Share:
A spectacular explosion of wildflowers has transformed the normally dry, rust-colored landscape of Western Australia into a vibrant patchwork of green and colorful blooms. The remarkable display followed months of unusually wet weather, awakening seeds that had been lying dormant beneath the soil.
By late winter 2026 in the Southern Hemisphere, large stretches of the region's arid shrubland were covered in flowers. Local experts believe this could be the most impressive wildflower season the area has experienced in nearly 20 years.
NASA satellite imagery reveals just how dramatically the landscape changed in a single year.
NASA Satellite Images Reveal a Dramatic Transformation
The images above were collected by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) aboard the NASA-USGS Landsat 8 satellite. They show the same part of Western Australia in late August 2025 (left) and late August 2026 (right), highlighting the striking increase in vegetation following the unusually wet conditions.
The location is in the Murchison region, approximately 600 kilometers (370 miles) north of Perth. This remote stretch of the Australian outback is an important grazing area for sheep and cattle, with a landscape typically dominated by hardy plants adapted to limited rainfall.
Much of the region's vegetation consists of grasses, saltbush, and mulga, a slow-growing evergreen tree capable of surviving in dry conditions. Wildflowers also emerge periodically, but their abundance can vary dramatically depending on how much rain falls.
Unusually Heavy Rains Trigger a Wildflower Explosion
The exceptional display in 2026 was made possible by a series of cold fronts that carried much-needed moisture into the region.
According to Australia's Bureau of Meteorology, June brought above-average rainfall, while August was much wetter than normal. These favorable conditions allowed seeds that had remained inactive in the dry soil to germinate, producing an extraordinary variety of wildflowers across the landscape.
The colorful transformation extended into the grounds of a radio astronomy observatory operated by the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), Australia's national science agency.
Among the flowers were several threatened species, adding ecological significance to the seasonal spectacle. The observatory has helped track these vulnerable plants on land that was previously used for livestock grazing.
Where Wildflowers Bloom Beneath Deep-Space Telescopes
While the flowers created an extraordinary scene on the ground, the observatory's usual work takes place far beyond Earth's atmosphere.
Known as Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-astronomy Observatory is a remote research facility dedicated to studying the universe through radio astronomy. Its antenna arrays detect radio signals from celestial objects, allowing scientists to observe and catalog sources across the southern sky.
The observatory's isolated location is particularly important for this work. It sits within a designated "radio quiet" zone, where communication systems and electronic equipment are restricted to reduce interference with sensitive scientific instruments.
Even relatively weak signals generated by human technology can interfere with radio observations, so limiting these disturbances helps astronomers detect faint emissions traveling across space.
Australia's Radio Telescopes Have Helped NASA Explore Space
Australia's radio astronomy facilities have a long history of supporting some of NASA's most important space missions.
The Murriyang radio telescope, located in Parkes, New South Wales, helped track Mariner 2 in 1962. That spacecraft became the first successful planetary science mission, marking a major milestone in the exploration of other worlds.
The telescope also played a significant role during the Apollo 11 Moon landing in 1969, serving as an important receiving station for communications from the historic mission.
CSIRO additionally manages the Canberra Deep Space Communication Complex, one of three major facilities that make up NASA's worldwide Deep Space Network.
This global system maintains communications with spacecraft traveling throughout the solar system and beyond, while also supporting radar measurements and radio astronomy research.
Both the Murriyang telescope and the Canberra complex contributed to NASA's Artemis II mission in April 2026, continuing Australia's decades-long involvement in space exploration.
For a brief period in 2026, however, one of Australia's most remote astronomical research regions offered a remarkable spectacle much closer to home. While its telescopes continued scanning the distant universe, unusually generous winter rains brought the surrounding outback to life in a brilliant display of wildflowers.
