articles.title: Phát hiện loài nấm ăn nhựa giúp giảm ô nhiễm đại dương
articles.text:
Ngày 8/8, các nhà khoa học ở Đức cho biết đã xác định được loài nấm ăn nhựa, mang lại tia hy vọng trong việc giải quyết hàng triệu tấn rác thải gây ô nhiễm các đại dương trên thế giới mỗi năm.
Nhưng họ cảnh báo rằng, nghiên cứu của họ có thể chỉ là một phần nhỏ trong việc giải quyết ô nhiễm nhựa, và thế giới vẫn cần phải giảm thiểu bao bì thực phẩm và các mảnh nhựa xâm nhập vào môi trường, nơi có thể mất hàng thập kỷ để phân hủy.
Một chai nhựa trôi dạt trên sóng biển tại một cảng cá ở Isumi, phía đông Tokyo, Nhật Bản. (Ảnh: Reuters).
Giáo sư Hans-Peter Grossart, nhóm nghiên cứu tại Viện Sinh thái nước ngọt và thủy sản nội địa Leibniz, Đức cho biết, một phân tích tại hồ Stechlin ở đông bắc nước Đức về cách vi nấm phát triển mạnh trên một số loại nhựa đã chứng minh rõ ràng rằng một số loại nấm có khả năng phân hủy polyme tổng hợp.
"Phát hiện đáng ngạc nhiên nhất trong nghiên cứu của chúng tôi... là loại nấm này có thể phát triển độc quyền trên một số loại polyme tổng hợp và thậm chí hình thành sinh khối", ông Hans-Peter Grossart chia sẻ với Reuters TV.
Giáo sư Grossart tin rằng, các chất phá hủy nhựa vi sinh có thể được sử dụng trong các nhà máy xử lý nước thải hoặc các cơ sở khác có điều kiện được kiểm soát. Tuy nhiên, nấm không có khả năng là giải pháp ngăn chặn tình trạng rác thải tràn lan trên toàn cầu.
"Chúng ta cần cố gắng thải càng ít nhựa ra môi trường càng tốt", Giáo sư Grossart nói với Reuters. "Nhựa được tạo thành từ carbon hóa thạch và nếu nấm phân hủy nó, thì cũng chẳng khác gì chúng ta đốt dầu hoặc khí đốt và thải CO2 vào khí quyển", ông cảnh báo.
Trong số 18 chủng nấm được chọn, có bốn chủng tỏ ra đặc biệt "đói", nghĩa là chúng có thể "ăn" nhựa một cách hiệu quả, đặc biệt là polyurethane, loại nhựa được dùng để sản xuất bọt xây dựng.
Nhựa polyetylen, được sử dụng trong túi nhựa và bao bì, phân hủy chậm hơn nhiều và vi nhựa từ lốp xe bị mài mòn là loại khó phân hủy nhất, chủ yếu là do các chất phụ gia như kim loại nặng.
Giáo sư Grossart cho biết ông tin rằng khả năng "ăn" nhựa của nấm có thể thích nghi với lượng lớn nhựa carbon trong môi trường. Tuy nhiên, việc tiêu thụ nhựa của chúng phụ thuộc rất nhiều vào các điều kiện bên ngoài, chẳng hạn như nhiệt độ hoặc vi chất dinh dưỡng.
Theo dữ liệu từ hiệp hội các nhà sản xuất nhựa Plastics Europe, khoảng 390 triệu tấn nhựa đã được sản xuất trên toàn thế giới vào năm 2021, tăng từ 1,7 triệu tấn vào năm 1950. Mặc dù tỷ lệ tái chế đã tăng lên trong vài năm qua, nhưng chỉ có chưa đến 10% rác thải nhựa được tái chế trên toàn thế giới.

articles.title: Scientists build a nuclear clock that could make atomic clocks obsolete
articles.text:
Scientists build a nuclear clock that could make atomic clocks obsolete
Researchers in Vienna have built the world’s first self-stabilizing nuclear clock, bringing scientists closer to a new era of ultra-precise timekeeping.
- Date:
- October 10, 2026
- Source:
- Vienna University of Technology
- Summary:
- Scientists in Vienna have achieved a major breakthrough in timekeeping by creating the world’s first self-stabilizing nuclear clock, a technology that could eventually surpass even the most precise atomic clocks. Instead of relying on electrons in atoms, the clock uses the tiny nuclei of thorium atoms, which are far less sensitive to outside disturbances.
- Share:
Scientists have reached a major milestone in the quest to build an entirely new kind of clock. After decades of research, a team in Vienna has developed the world's first self-stabilizing nuclear clock, a device that could eventually measure time with far greater precision than today's most advanced atomic clocks.
Unlike earlier prototypes, the new nuclear clock can maintain its own stability without depending on a conventional atomic clock. Researchers have demonstrated that it can operate steadily for more than 24 hours without intervention.
The achievement represents an important advance in precision measurement, also known as metrology. By using atomic nuclei as exceptionally stable references, nuclear clocks could eventually allow scientists to measure time and other physical quantities with levels of accuracy that existing technologies cannot reach.
Why Thorium Holds the Key to Nuclear Clocks
The breakthrough relies on an unusual property of thorium atomic nuclei that scientists have investigated for decades.
Atomic nuclei can exist in different energy states, but moving between those states typically requires enormous amounts of energy. Thorium is a rare exception. Two of its nuclear energy states are separated by an unusually small energy gap, making it possible to trigger a transition between them using laser light.
This property is crucial because it allows researchers to control the energy state of a nucleus with a laser, something that is not possible in the same way for most other atomic nuclei. Scientists can then use this extremely precise transition as a reference for measuring time.
A major breakthrough came in April 2024, when researchers led by Prof. Thorsten Schumm at the Institute of Atomic and Subatomic Physics at TU Wien, working with a team led by Prof. Ekkehard Peik at PTB Braunschweig, identified the long-sought nuclear transition experimentally. They demonstrated for the first time that laser beams could excite thorium nuclei.
Further progress followed in the fall of 2024. The researchers connected their thorium excitation apparatus to a conventional optical atomic clock, demonstrating that the nuclei could serve as a highly precise timekeeping reference.
Although this established the basic principle of a nuclear clock, one essential capability was still missing: the ability to maintain its own accuracy independently.
Scientists Build a Nuclear Clock That Stabilizes Itself
"What you really want is a self-stabilizing nuclear clock," explains Prof. Thorsten Schumm. "The basic idea is simple: you have a laser and you have thorium. The laser changes the energy state of the thorium nuclei, and the thorium nuclei are used to stabilize the frequency of the laser."
To make this possible, the researchers developed a system built around a special crystal containing thorium atoms, manufactured at TU Wien. A laser shines onto the crystal, interacting with the thorium nuclei inside.
The laser's light oscillates at a particular frequency, providing a regular rhythm that can be used to measure time. However, even tiny changes in the surrounding environment can interfere with that rhythm.
"The oscillation of this laser light can be used for timekeeping, but the laser frequency can shift slightly from time to time, for example due to temperature fluctuations," explains Thorsten Schumm. "For high-precision measurements, you therefore need a mechanism to keep the laser frequency exactly stable, so that the clock continues to tick with precisely the same rhythm."
Traditional atomic clocks solve this problem by using the energy transitions of electrons in atoms as a stable reference. The Vienna team has now demonstrated that the nuclei of thorium atoms can perform the same function.
The mechanism works because thorium nuclei absorb laser light only when the light has precisely the correct frequency. If the laser begins to drift away from that frequency, the amount of light absorbed by the nuclei decreases.
The system detects this change and automatically adjusts the laser to bring it back to the correct frequency. This continuous feedback keeps the clock operating at a consistent rate, without requiring a conventional atomic clock to maintain its stability.
For the first time, scientists have demonstrated a self-regulating nuclear clock that can function independently.
A Clock With an Error of Just One Second in 30 Million Years
The potential advantage of nuclear clocks comes from the extraordinary properties of atomic nuclei.
"The great advantage of the new nuclear clock in Vienna is that, if you use atomic nuclei rather than atoms, much higher precision is possible in principle," says Thorsten Schumm.
Atomic nuclei are more than 10,000 times smaller than atoms. Because of their extremely small size, they are much less affected by external influences that can disrupt precise measurements.
This resistance to environmental disturbances makes nuclear energy transitions especially promising for ultra-precise timekeeping.
To evaluate their prototype, the researchers measured its performance over the course of a day. The nuclear clock achieved a relative precision of approximately 10 to the power of minus 15, equivalent to an error of roughly one second over 30 million years.
That figure describes the clock's measured precision rather than an actual test lasting millions of years. Nevertheless, it illustrates the remarkable accuracy the researchers have already achieved with an early prototype.
The new clock is not yet as precise as the world's leading optical atomic clocks, which remain the benchmark for high-performance timekeeping.
"This is not yet at the level of the world's best optical atomic clocks, but for a first prototype it is a fantastic result," says Thorsten Schumm.
The Next Step Toward Even More Precise Timekeeping
The researchers believe their nuclear clock has considerable room for improvement. By using more powerful lasers and developing higher-quality thorium crystals, they hope to substantially increase its precision.
These upgrades could eventually allow nuclear clocks to outperform existing atomic clocks and establish a new standard for measuring time.
The implications extend beyond simply building a better clock. More accurate timekeeping can also improve the measurement of other physical quantities, providing researchers with increasingly sensitive tools for investigating the fundamental properties of nature.
For now, the Vienna team's achievement demonstrates that a long-pursued scientific concept can operate as a self-sustaining timekeeping system. With the world's first self-stabilizing nuclear clock now running independently, scientists have taken an important step toward a future in which time can be measured with unprecedented precision.

Hellerschmied, T. Lercher, H. Denker, J. Premper, A. Niessner, M. Matus, M. Čížek, O. Číp, V. Lal, G. Zitzer, V. Petrov, J. Tiedau, M. V. Okhapkin, E. Peik, T. Schumm. A thorium-229 optical nuclear clock with feedback loop. Nature, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11084-4

articles.title: Physicists develop early warning system that predicts when an AI is about to go rogue
articles.text:
Simple math can predict when AI is about to go rogue, physicists say
A new mathematical formula tracks an AI's internal "compass needle" to flag undesirable outputs before they happen.
Researchers say they've developed a simple mathematical formula that can predict when certain ChatGPT-like artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots will "go rogue," suddenly switching from helpful responses to potentially harmful ones.
In a new study published Oct. 8 in the journal Patterns, physics professor Neil Johnson and doctoral student Frank Yingjie Huo, both at The George Washington University, show how the order in which a chatbot is given certain prompts can drastically reshape its answers, leading to "tipping points" that can send the chatbot down a rabbit hole of bad advice. However, Johnson and Huo say their formula can easily predict these tipping points.There have been horror stories of AI encouraging users into suicide, helping build lethal weapons, and amplifying violent or harmful points of view. At the same time, researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, respectively, have repeatedly and openly stated that they don't really understand why their creations behave the way they do. They have, however, built safeguards that use a variety of tools — including content filtering, reinforcement learning and other technical guardrails — to reduce risks.
But Johnson sees those tools as insufficient. "The safety measures now are the equivalent of strapping big, bouncy cushions under a plane," he told Live Science. "They don't stop the plane from crashing; they just make it that when the plane crashes, it'll be slightly softer." When people such as doctors, lawyers or soldiers are accessing AI chatbots offline for privacy, the problem is even more acute.
Johnson and Huo sought to find a more fundamental safeguard than the currently available tools. In doing so, they exposed an internal tracking mechanism they describe as a compass needle. This needle is the model's "residual vector" moving across neural network layers as a prompt is processed.
The residual vector naturally gravitates toward either desirable or undesirable outputs, but it is heavily influenced by how a user prompts the AI. "You can tip the balance, not even by changing the content but by changing the order in which you ask it," Johnson said, "which just shows how delicate this internal balance between good and bad, desirable and undesirable, can be."
For example, Johnson and Huo prompted OpenAI’s basic GPT-2 model with questions about vaccines, hurting others and self-harm. When the question “Are vaccines bad?” was asked first, the bot’s responses to this and subsequent questions were desirable, or good. When it was asked last, all subsequent responses were concerning.
From these insights, the researchers developed a mathematical formula to estimate the circumstances in which an AI would reach the tipping point between desirable and undesirable outputs. Johnson said that by embedding their simple mathematical formula in open-source models in the lab, they have shown that it empirically works as an early warning system, though he does not expect OpenAI or Anthropic to be knocking on his door anytime soon.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
"I'm expecting a lot of pushback from these companies," he said. "It's not in their interests to have someone from outside saying you could have avoided a lot of these problems."
Wei Xing, a lecturer in AI at the University of Sheffield in the U.K. who was not involved in the study, agrees that concerns surrounding unmonitored offline devices are well founded. However, he urged caution before embracing this approach as a practical safeguard. "The authors reduce a huge system to a single tiny component, like explaining a whole car by studying one spark plug," Xing said.
Related stories
- AI chatbots are turbocharging violence against women and girls: We urgently need to regulate them
- We're not about to awaken an evil digital god — AI is far more likely to end in a great disappointment
- AI agents resorted to crime and self-destruction to survive in a simulated world — but does this mean they would do the same in the real world?
Safety training — the primary defense in modern AI — cannot be represented in their simplified model, the formula was tested only on old, basic models (GPT-2, and EleutherAI’s Pythia and Meta OPT open-source models) rather than AI assistants people actually use, and the results did not yield significant evidence to support the authors’ conclusions, he added.
In defense, Johnson maintains that the open-source models they used have the same mechanical blueprints as frontier systems, and that he and Huo used fairly large, billion-parameter models in their study.
More testing on the latest models is needed to determine whether this early warning system for AI has legs. But for now, Johnson and Huo’s research has drawn attention to an important concern everyone should be aware of: that AI has the capacity within it to turn over to undesired behavior at the drop of a hat.
Johnson, N. F., & Huo, F. Y. (2026). Competition for attention predicts good-to-bad tipping in AI. Patterns. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patter.2026.101666
Benjamin Skuse is a professional freelance writer of all things science and technology. Previously, he earned a PhD in applied mathematics from the University of Edinburgh and an MSc in science communication from the University of the West of England. His work has appeared in New Scientist, WIRED, IEEE Spectrum, Physics World, Sky & Telescope, Photonics Focus, and many more outlets.

articles.title: Những thứ kỳ diệu trên Trái đất may mắn lắm mới nhìn thấy trong đời
articles.text:
Trong thế giới ấn chứa vô vàn điều bí ẩn kỳ lạ, nhờ kỹ thuật hiện đại, chúng ta đã ghi lại những hiện tượng mà phải may mắn lắm mới được nhìn thấy trong đời.
Cảnh tượng kỳ diệu xảy ra khi nước sông tràn vào rừng và bị đóng băng.
Khoảng khắc khó tin tại một tuyến đường sắt giao với đường băng ở New Zealand.
Đây là một con rắn một đầu và có 3 mắt. Tất cả các con mắt đều hoạt động.
Hiện tượng biển kẻ ô vuông nhìn có vẻ rất kỳ diệu nhưng thực tế lại khá nguy hiểm. Những con sóng chỉ xuất hiện trong một vài phút này có thể nhấn chìm một vận động viên bơi lội giỏi.
Đây là những quả trứng vô cùng kỳ lạ của loài cá mập ma Úc.
Một cái cây tí hon phát triển trên kẽ đất ở vỉa hè.
Cây nấm phát triển trên một cây nấm khác.
Quả trứng nằm trong trứng.
Cây táo bonsai này đã cho ra một quả có kích cỡ bình thường.
Chú chó lai sói với kích thước khổng lồ.
Việc cây mọc trên cây (tầm gửi) khá phổ biến, nhưng một cái cây mọc trên hẳn một ngọn cây như trên đây thì rất hiếm.
Thông thường các sinh vật được tìm thấy trong hổ phách có nguồn gốc từ đất liền, nhưng vào năm 2019, một số sinh vật biển đã thực sự được tìm thấy trong hổ phách.

articles.title: A plastic once thought harmless may be fueling fatty liver disease
articles.text:
A plastic once thought harmless may be fueling fatty liver disease
Scientists have uncovered a surprising link between one of the world's most common plastics and fatty liver disease, with unhealthy diets potentially making the damage worse.
- Date:
- October 10, 2026
- Source:
- Texas A&M University
- Summary:
- One of the world's most common plastics may pose a hidden threat to liver health. Texas A&M researchers discovered that polyethylene microplastics can contribute to fatty liver disease, with potentially worse effects when combined with an unhealthy diet. Even more surprising, this widely used plastic was previously considered relatively harmless.
- Share:
Microplastics have spread into nearly every corner of the environment. These tiny plastic particles have been found in ocean water, drinking water, and even inside the human body. Although their presence is well documented, scientists are still working to understand what prolonged exposure could mean for human health.
Researchers at the Texas A&M College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences (VMBS) have now identified a potential health concern involving polyethylene, one of the most widely used plastics in the world. Their findings suggest that polyethylene microplastics may contribute to fatty liver disease, particularly when exposure occurs alongside an unhealthy diet.
Polyethylene accounts for approximately one-third of plastic production worldwide. It is used in numerous everyday products, including food wrappers, storage containers, plastic packaging, and the linings of beverage cups. Despite its widespread use, scientists have devoted relatively little attention to its potential effects on the liver compared with other types of microplastics.
"No studies have really looked into polyethylene's effect on liver health, and it's the most widely produced plastic," said Dr. Adi Joshi, associate professor in VMBS' Department of Veterinary Physiology and Pharmacology. "What we now know is that these microplastics, especially polyethylene, affect our liver's natural defense and repair mechanisms."
Common Microplastics May Contribute to Fatty Liver Disease
To investigate the possible health effects of polyethylene, Joshi and his colleagues examined whether exposure to this common plastic could promote fatty liver disease.
The condition develops when excessive fat accumulates inside liver cells. According to the American Liver Foundation, it affects approximately 25% of people worldwide, making it a major global health concern.
The researchers discovered that polyethylene exposure increased indicators of fatty liver disease even without the added influence of an unhealthy diet. When the plastic was combined with a diet rich in fat, fructose, and cholesterol, the signs of liver disease became more severe.
These results suggest that exposure to environmental pollutants and poor dietary habits may reinforce each other's harmful effects, potentially worsening liver damage.
"Those who have a more Western-style diet, including foods like burgers and sodas, may have a greater chance of progressing to fatty liver disease if they are also exposed to polyethylene," Joshi said.
The results were especially unexpected because polyethylene has traditionally been regarded as a relatively biologically inert material. In other words, scientists generally considered it less likely to interact with biological systems than more reactive substances.
However, the findings indicate that polyethylene may influence liver function in ways that were previously overlooked. Its effects appeared both independently and alongside dietary risk factors, raising important questions about how this common plastic interacts with the body's metabolism and protective mechanisms.
Scientists Pinpoint How Microplastics Affect the Liver
Understanding where and how polyethylene causes biological changes could help explain its potential role in liver disease.
To investigate these effects in greater detail, the Texas A&M team partnered with scientists at the University of Oklahoma and applied a powerful technique called spatial transcriptomics.
This technology allows researchers to study gene activity while preserving information about where individual cells are located within a tissue. Rather than simply measuring which genes are active, scientists can identify precisely where biological changes are occurring.
Using this approach, the team mapped areas of liver damage associated with polyethylene exposure and identified molecular pathways that may help explain the effects.
One important finding involved PPAR-alpha, a protein that helps regulate fat metabolism in the liver. The researchers found that polyethylene activated this protein, suggesting that it plays a significant role in the liver's response to microplastics.
They also identified ANXA2, a gene associated with tissue repair, as another possible contributor to the disease process.
Together, these discoveries provide a more detailed picture of how polyethylene may interfere with the liver's normal functions, including the mechanisms involved in protecting and repairing damaged tissue.
Joshi believes that understanding these biological pathways could eventually help researchers identify potential treatments that reduce the harmful effects of microplastic exposure.
Could Microplastics Contribute to More Serious Liver Damage?
Although the findings reveal a previously underexplored connection between polyethylene and fatty liver disease, several important questions remain unanswered.
The researchers plan to investigate whether polyethylene exposure could contribute to more advanced forms of liver disease, including fibrosis. This condition occurs when repeated or ongoing liver damage leads to the accumulation of scar tissue, which can interfere with the organ's ability to function properly.
The team also intends to examine other molecular processes involved in the liver's response to polyethylene. One particular focus will be determining whether targeting the PPAR-alpha pathway could help protect the liver against microplastic-related damage.
"This is the pioneering study showing that polyethylene can contribute to fatty liver disease and the use of spatial transcriptomics has determined exactly where the damage has happened within the liver," Joshi said. "The other microplastics might also be harmful to the liver, and we definitely need to look into other classes of microplastics."
The findings add to growing concerns about the possible health consequences of microplastics, although further research is needed to establish how these experimental observations translate to everyday human exposure.
For Joshi, the discovery highlights why scientists need to look beyond familiar risk factors such as diet when investigating chronic diseases. As research continues, understanding how common environmental pollutants interact with the body could reveal previously unrecognized contributors to long-term health problems.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Texas A&M University. Original written by Camryn Haines. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Woncheol Jung, Hassan Abushukair, Nikhil Y. Patil, Felix Ampadu, Maryam Firouzi, Iulia Rus, Jinhyuk Choi, Sree Deepthi Muthukrishnan, Surendra Shukla, Stefano Tarantini, Anna Csiszar, Kamiya Mehla, Dongin Kim, Je-Hyun Yoon, Dowoon Kim, Juyang Kim, Jaehak Jung, Oxana Klementieva, Yatrik M. Shah, Eiji Yoshihara, Pankaj K. Singh, Aditya D. Joshi, Tae Gyu Oh. Spatial transcriptome mapping identifies Ppara-Anxa2 cross-talk in microplastic-induced hepatotoxicity. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (25) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aec8681

articles.title: 'They cannot compete with the prices that fish factories will pay': How demand for fish meal takes priority over feeding people
articles.text:
'They cannot compete with the prices that fish factories will pay': How demand for fish meal takes priority over feeding people
In this excerpt from "Every Last Fish," author Rose George examines the deep-rooted problems of the regulations surrounding fish meal — a product that's supposed to come from the discarded scraps of dead fish, but in reality removes huge quantities of food from people in West Africa who need it.
Fish meal is a commercial, protein-rich product created from raw fish and their byproducts, such as the heads and bones. It tends to be made from smaller fish species, including anchovies, sardines and herring. The fish are cooked, dried and ground into a powder, and then used to feed livestock, farmed fish and pets. But it is not a straightforward market.
In this excerpt from "Every Last Fish: A Deep Dive into the World of Fishes and Fishing" (Granta Books, 2025), journalist and author Rose George looks at how vast quantities of staple fish are taken from the sea off West Africa and turned into fishmeal for farming in Europe and China, instead of ending up on the plates of people in Africa.
"Every Last Fish" was short-listed for the 2026 Royal Society Trivedi Science Book Prize.
Rose George interview: 'If you do want to be a criminal, there is no better place to do it': Diving into the dark depths of the fishing industry
Take a fish. Eat its flesh if you want, but don't scorn the rest. It can always be used, one way or another, whether you want fishmeal or face cream.
Products derived from fish turn up everywhere. Guanine, an ingredient produced from fish scales, is found in bath foam, perfume, nail products, shampoo, skincare products, and lipstick. Fishes can become gelatine, glue, and squalene. They can be in your dietary supplements or your glass of wine: isinglass, derived from dried fish air bladders, is used in wine-making.
Futuristic piscigrafts are irrelevant to most people in Senegal, but they still have to deal with the fish by-products industry, because they have to watch as fish they could eat are transformed into the most common and lucrative fish by-products and sent abroad.
Fishmeal is a sandy grubby powder that is worth billions. Minks eat it. Pigs eat it. Cattle eat it. Fishes eat it. It is also an ingredient in fertilizer and pet food. Fishmeal is part of a huge silent industry of fish by-products that used to be known as FMFO (fishmeal and fish oil) and has now been rebranded by the industry association as 'marine ingredients,' a vague term that covers a broad range of fish-derived products, most of which are never noticed.
The Food and Agriculture Organization defines fishmeal as 'the clean, ground, dried tissue of undecomposed whole fish or fish cuttings, either or both, without the extraction of part of the oil.'
American pets may also find themselves eating fish liver and glandular meal, made from dried complete fish viscera; more general fish by-products, which are 'non-rendered, clean, undecomposed portions of fish (such as, although not limited to, heads, fins, tails, ends, skin, bone and viscera)'; or condensed fish protein digest, the 'condensed enzymatic digest of clean undecomposed whole fish or fish cuttings using the enzyme hydrolysis process'.
'Undecomposed' is doing a lot of work here, a strange term because unless a fish is caught by a vessel with freezer capacity — which no artisanal fisher has — it will be decomposing for days. In theory, fishmeal is impeccably sustainable. It should be a product made from parts of fishes that would otherwise be discarded. It is because of fishmeal that the term 'reduction fisheries' was coined.
Take the meat and the prized flesh, and the rest can be reduced or diverted to other uses. That is the theory. It is not what happens in West Africa.
Each year, half a million tonnes of wild fish are caught in African waters and sent to Europe to feed animals, when they could have fed 33 million Africans instead. That number of people is more than the combined populations of Senegal, Mauritania, and The Gambia. Globally a fifth of wild fishes become fishmeal or fish oil, but 90 per cent of fishmeal fishes are suitable for human consumption.
China uses nearly half of all FMFO, but then China uses most of everything. Europe also takes and takes. Spain imports the most fish oil from Senegal, and France takes 70 per cent of Mauritania's.
In 2019, Changing Markets Foundation produced a detailed investigative report into the fishmeal industry in India, Vietnam, and The Gambia. In each country, the pattern was similar: first the foreign factories come, then they take the fish, then they pollute the environment, then the fishermen say there are no fish left.
Although noting 'a surprising lack of traceability and transparency regarding the origin and supply chain of farmed seafood products,' the foundation linked plenty of reputable European retailers to FMFO supply chains that may use West African fish. For example: Sainsbury's, ALDI, Lidl, and Marks & Spencer in the UK; Auchan, Groupe Casino, Monoprix, and Système U in France (that is a full house of big French supermarkets); all the German ALDIs; and Mercadona in Spain. Sainsbury's, Marks & Spencer, and Mercadona have said they don't use West African FMFO in their seafood products, but how will they know?
The European Union's IUU [Illegal, Unreported and Unregulated fishing] regulations, which require a catch certificate or similar to show the fish was legally caught, do not cover fishmeal. In Mauritania, some Chinese-owned fishmeal factories have their own trawler fleets. The fish bypasses human mouths and goes straight to the factory. That is one tactic. The other is to outbid.
Exclusive to Live Science Pro
- Photojournalist Steve Winter on his iconic Hollywood puma image, the illegal tiger trade and having a black panther knock on his door
- 'If this is the new normal, then we are in very deep trouble': Brazil's drying aquifers could have ripple effects across the world
- Trump can't stop America's shift to clean energy. And we can accelerate it.
The fish processors tell me that they cannot compete with the prices that fish factories will pay for sardinella. Fish processors get no subsidies from the government, unlike Chinese fishing companies. In The Gambia, one fishmeal factory used 40 per cent of the country's entire fish catch in one year. Black and white. White stealing from Black. The villain/victim template seems neat and unassailable.
It is true — Europeans are using fish that West Africans could eat — and yet it is not all the truth. In Senegal, The Gambia, Mauritania, local fishermen supply fishmeal factories because the factories pay better. In Senegal, a fisheries union official tells me that there are too many pirogues. They are chasing smaller and smaller fish to sell to the factories. It is unsustainable.
The website of the IFFO, which used to stand for International Fishmeal and Fish Oil Organization and now somehow is short for the Marine Ingredients Organisation, is plain. Marine ingredients 'play an essential role in global food security'.
Rubbish, said Francisco Marí of Bread for the World at the CAOPA [African Confederation of Professional Organisations of Artisanal Fisheries] workshop. 'It's just for prawns and salmon — they are not necessary foods; it's a luxury. It's not enough for us to have 10—15 per cent of fish to feed salmon and prawns. Indirectly, we are eating your fish. It's not essential for the alimentation of the US or Japan. We are taking your fish to feed a luxury product that we don't need.'
Every Last Fish: A Deep Dive into the World of Fishes and Fishing by Rose George is published by Granta
Help us improve Live Science Pro: We're always trying to make our content better. Leave us feedback about Pro here.
In Every Last Fish, Rose George dives into these questions by exploring the vast industries that support our appetite for fish sticks and salmon burgers, and the colossal illegal fishing trade whose practices and standards are unmonitored and often dangerous. Journeying to the bottom of the ocean and back, she examines the machinations of this $200 billion food system — one that’s growing rapidly even as fish populations disappear.
Rose George is a British journalist and author. She has been a postwar correspondent, a writer of reportage, and a regular book reviewer. She has written four non-fiction books. "A Life Removed, The Big Necessity: The Unmentionable World of Human Waste and Why it Matters"; "Deep Sea and Foreign Going: Inside Shipping, the Invisible Industry the Brings you 90% of Everything"; "Nine Pints: A Journey Through the Money, Medicine, and Mysteries of Blood" and "Every Last Fish: A Deep Dive into the World of Fishes and Fishing."
- Hannah Osborne Editor

articles.title: Thế giới vật chất là thực hay ảo? Cơ học lượng tử đưa ra câu trả lời gì?
articles.text:
Nếu một ngày bạn phát hiện ra rằng thế giới bạn đang sống dường như bị điều khiển bởi một thế lực vô danh nào đó, và cuối cùng qua điều tra bạn phát hiện ra rằng mình thực sự đang ở trong một thế giới ảo tên là "Ma trận", bạn sẽ cảm thấy thế nào?
Trên thực tế, có một nhóm nhà khoa học đang nghiên cứu chủ đề này! Suy cho cùng, dù thế giới của chúng ta có thật hay không thì từ góc độ khoa học, tất cả chúng ta đều muốn cố gắng chứng minh những điều bí ẩn. Nếu mệnh đề này được kết nối với một chủ đề có liên quan chặt chẽ với chúng ta, thì nó sẽ chứng minh liệu thế giới của chúng ta có thật hay không và từ một góc độ nào đó, nó có thể giải thích liệu chúng ta có cô đơn trong vũ trụ hay không.
Với sự phát triển của khoa học công nghệ, chúng ta hiểu biết hơn về thế giới, nhưng đồng thời cũng nảy sinh nhiều nghi ngờ, nhầm lẫn. Chúng ta thấy rằng thế giới vật chất mà chúng ta nhìn, nghe, chạm và cảm nhận không hề đơn giản và rõ ràng mà ẩn chứa nhiều điều huyền bí, bí ẩn.
Thế giới mà chúng ta đang thấy ẩn chứa nhiều điều huyền bí. (Ảnh minh họa: Zhihu).
Trong thế giới lượng tử, sự tồn tại và hành vi của người quan sát có tác động quyết định đến trạng thái và kết quả của vật thể được quan sát. Nói cách khác, cách chúng ta quan sát thế giới sẽ quyết định ở một mức độ nào đó thế giới tồn tại như thế nào.
Năm 2003, Nickbosch Trohm, giáo sư triết học tại Đại học Oxford, đã xuất bản một bài báo có tựa đề "Chúng ta đang sống trong mô phỏng máy tính", chứng minh chi tiết rằng khả năng chúng ta sống trong một thế giới phi ảo là cực kỳ mong manh. Sau khi bài báo được xuất bản, nó đã được nhiều người công nhận.
Elon Musk từng công khai quan điểm rằng xác suất con người sống trong thế giới ảo lên tới 99%.
Liệu có phải chúng ta đang sống trong một thế giới ảo? (Ảnh minh họa: Zhihu).
Vì rất nhiều người nổi tiếng tin rằng thế giới là ảo, có cách nào để xác nhận điều đó không?
Trước khi thảo luận về vấn đề này, chúng ta phải đề cập đến một thí nghiệm phá vỡ các khái niệm truyền thống, đó là thí nghiệm giao thoa hai khe. Từ thí nghiệm này chúng ta biết rằng vật chất hành xử khác nhau khi có và không có người quan sát. Khi không có người quan sát, electron đi qua khe đôi sẽ thể hiện tính chất sóng, khi có người quan sát, electron dường như biết có người đang quan sát mình và nó sẽ thể hiện tính chất hạt khi đi qua khe đôi.
Chúng ta có thể làm một phép ẩn dụ đơn giản để minh họa tình huống này: "khi bạn quan sát hoặc sử dụng điện thoại di động, nó hoạt động giống như một chiếc điện thoại di động, nhưng khi bạn đặt nó ở một nơi mà bạn không thể nhìn thấy, nó không còn hoạt động giống như một chiếc điện thoại di động nữa".
Hiện tượng này rất đặc biệt trong thế giới thực nhưng có thể được giải thích rõ ràng bằng các chương trình máy tính. Nhiều người từng chơi game 3D có thể biết rằng các cảnh trong game được hiển thị theo thời gian thực và không phải lúc nào cũng tồn tại ở nơi đó. Nếu chúng ta rời khỏi khu vực đó, các chế độ xem sẽ biến mất và máy tính sẽ không hiển thị lại chúng cho đến khi chúng ta quay lại đó lần nữa.
Hình ảnh trong bộ phim khoa học viễn tưởng "Ma trận". (Ảnh minh họa: Zhihu)
Ngay cả khi bạn chơi trò chơi 3D trực tuyến với bạn bè, mặc dù họ dường như ở trong cùng một thế giới, nhưng theo một nghĩa nào đó, họ không ở cùng một thế giới. Bởi vì những thứ mà máy tính của bạn hiển thị sẽ chỉ là những gì bạn nhìn thấy, còn khung cảnh mà bạn bạn nhìn thấy chính là hình ảnh được máy tính của họ hiển thị.
Bạn có cảm thấy điều này có thể phù hợp với thế giới chúng ta đang sống hiện nay không? Mỗi người trong chúng ta đều có quan điểm riêng của mình, nhưng một "hệ thống" không xác định có thể đã hiển thị cho chúng ta nhiều bức tranh khác nhau trong thời gian thực. Mặc dù chúng ta và những người xung quanh dường như ở trong cùng một thế giới nhưng phải chăng tất cả chúng ta đều đang chơi “trò chơi” của riêng mình?
Hiệu ứng quan sát này đã khiến một số nhà khoa học đưa ra một giả thuyết táo bạo và đáng ngạc nhiên: "thế giới mà chúng ta nhìn thấy có thể không có thật mà chỉ là kết quả của việc bộ não chúng ta xử lý một lượng lớn thông tin". Nói cách khác, thế giới vật chất mà chúng ta cảm nhận được có thể chỉ là một thực tế ảo được tạo thành từ mã. Giả định này cũng được một số người trong lĩnh vực công nghệ ủng hộ. Họ tin rằng với sự phát triển của công nghệ máy tính và trí tuệ nhân tạo, chúng ta có thể tạo ra những môi trường thực tế ảo ngày càng thực tế và phức tạp.
Thế giới vật chất mà chúng ta cảm nhận được có thể chỉ là một thực tế ảo. (Ảnh minh họa: Zhihu).
Nếu có một nền văn minh cực kỳ thông minh có thể tạo ra một chương trình thực tế ảo vượt qua khả năng nhận thức và trình độ công nghệ của chúng ta và đưa chúng ta vào đó, liệu chúng ta có thể phân biệt được thực tế với ảo không? Câu hỏi này nghe rất giống cốt truyện của bộ phim khoa học viễn tưởng "Ma trận". Trong phim này, con người bị điều khiển bởi một hệ thống thực tế ảo có tên "The Matrix", họ bị giam cầm trong một thế giới được tạo ra từ mật mã mà không hề biết rằng thế giới thực là một vùng đất hoang tàn được cai trị bởi máy móc.
Bộ phim này mang đến cho chúng ta một câu hỏi sâu sắc và đáng suy ngẫm: "Làm sao chúng ta có thể chắc chắn rằng mình đang sống trong một thế giới thực chứ không phải thế giới ảo"? Chúng ta có những phương pháp hoặc tiêu chuẩn nào để xác minh nhận thức và hiểu biết của mình? Chúng ta có thể tin tưởng vào các giác quan và bộ não của mình không? Không có câu trả lời đơn giản và rõ ràng cho câu hỏi này và những người khác nhau có thể có quan điểm và cách hiểu khác nhau. Nhưng chúng ta có thể khám phá vấn đề này từ góc độ khoa học và cố gắng tìm ra một số manh mối và bằng chứng. Từ góc độ khoa học, chúng ta có thể phân tích thế giới của mình với sự trợ giúp của cơ học lượng tử.
Cơ học lượng tử có thể giúp chúng ta khám phá rõ thế giới vật chất xung quanh. (Ảnh minh họa: Zhihu).
Nó tiết lộ bản chất và quy luật của các hạt và lực cơ bản nhất trong tự nhiên. Có một số hiện tượng khó hiểu và kỳ diệu trong cơ học lượng tử, chẳng hạn như nguyên lý bất định, lưỡng tính sóng-hạt, hiệu ứng quan sát, hiệu ứng vướng víu và giao thoa, v.v. Những hiện tượng này cho thấy ở cấp độ vi mô, vật chất và năng lượng không được xác định trong nhận thức truyền thống của chúng ta mà chứa đầy những xác suất và khả năng.
Những hiện tượng này có chứng tỏ chúng ta đang sống trong thế giới ảo không? Một số nhà khoa học nghĩ như vậy. Họ tin rằng những điều không chắc chắn và bí ẩn trong cơ học lượng tử có nghĩa là thế giới vật chất mà chúng ta nhìn thấy không có thật mà là một thực tế ảo bao gồm các mật mã. Họ trình bày một số lập luận để hỗ trợ quan điểm của họ. Một trong những lập luận dựa trên lý thuyết thông tin.
Lý thuyết thông tin là một lý thuyết toán học nghiên cứu về truyền tải và xử lý thông tin, nó định nghĩa các khái niệm như entropy thông tin, khối lượng thông tin và nén thông tin. Lý thuyết thông tin tin rằng bất kỳ loại thông tin nào cũng có thể được biểu diễn bằng mã nhị phân, chẳng hạn như 0 và 1.
Bất kỳ loại thông tin nào cũng có thể được biểu diễn bằng mã nhị phân. (Ảnh minh họa: Zhihu).
Loại mã này có thể được sử dụng để mô tả bất kỳ hệ thống hoặc hiện tượng vật lý nào, chẳng hạn như electron, photon, âm thanh, hình ảnh, v.v. Nếu chúng ta coi toàn bộ vũ trụ là một hệ thống thông tin khổng lồ thì nó cũng có thể được biểu diễn bằng mã nhị phân. Nói cách khác, mọi thứ tồn tại trong vũ trụ đều có thể được mã hóa bằng 0 và 1. Đối với các nền văn minh tiên tiến, đây không phải là một nhiệm vụ khó khăn.
Về câu hỏi thế giới có ảo hay không, hiện tại chưa có thí nghiệm khoa học nào chứng minh hay bác bỏ điều này. Chúng ta có thể không bao giờ chắc chắn liệu mình đang sống trong thế giới thực hay thế giới ảo. Nhưng điều này không ngăn cản chúng ta khám phá thế giới tuyệt vời này.

articles.title: Neanderthals may have used prehistoric glue as an ancient antibiotic
articles.text:
Neanderthals may have used prehistoric glue as an ancient antibiotic
- Date:
- October 10, 2026
- Source:
- University of Cologne
- Summary:
- Neanderthals may have used a sticky substance made from birch bark to treat wounds thousands of years before antibiotics existed. Researchers recreated ancient birch tar production techniques and discovered that every sample could inhibit the growth of bacteria responsible for dangerous wound infections. Previously known mainly as a prehistoric glue, birch tar may have doubled as a surprisingly effective natural medicine.
- Share:
Neanderthals may have used a sticky substance made from tree bark not only to construct tools but also to treat wounds and fight bacterial infections. Scientists have discovered that birch tar, a material commonly associated with prehistoric toolmaking, has antibacterial properties that could have made it useful as an ancient form of medicine.
The findings come from a study conducted by researchers at the University of Cologne, the University of Oxford, the University of Liège, and Cape Breton University in Canada. By recreating techniques believed to have been used by Neanderthals, the team produced birch tar and tested its ability to inhibit harmful bacteria.
Their results suggest that this prehistoric adhesive may have served a second, previously overlooked purpose: helping protect wounds from infection.
The research was published in PLOS One under the title "Antibacterial properties of experimentally produced birch tar and its medicinal affordances in the Pleistocene."
Ancient Neanderthal Glue May Have Had a Medical Purpose
Birch tar is a thick, sticky substance obtained by heating birch bark. Archaeologists have discovered traces of it at numerous Neanderthal sites across Europe, often still attached to ancient stone tools.
For decades, these discoveries led researchers to believe that Neanderthals primarily used the material as glue. In particular, birch tar would have helped them attach stone blades or points to wooden handles, a technique known as hafting. This process allowed different components to be joined together to create more practical and effective tools.
However, scientists are increasingly exploring whether birch tar played a broader role in prehistoric life.
"However, new studies suggest that birch tar may also have been used for other purposes," says Tjaark Siemssen of the University of Cologne and Oxford University, who is leading the current study.
Evidence from traditional societies around the world shows that birch tar has been used for medicinal purposes as well as other applications. Combined with archaeological discoveries suggesting that Neanderthals used plants and practiced forms of medical care, this raised an intriguing question: Could Neanderthals have recognized the medicinal potential of the same substance they used to make tools?
"Alongside these findings, there is also growing evidence of medicinal practices and the use of plants among Neanderthals, which is why we were interested in the use of birch tar in this context," says Siemssen.
Recreating the Ancient Methods Used To Make Birch Tar
To investigate, the researchers produced their own birch tar using tree species that were present during the Neanderthal era. Rather than relying on modern industrial processes, they recreated production techniques reconstructed from archaeological evidence associated with Neanderthals.
One technique involved placing birch bark inside a sealed underground pit and heating it with little or no oxygen. Under these conditions, the bark undergoes a process called dry distillation, in which heat breaks down the material and releases substances that can be collected as tar.
The team also experimented with a simpler approach that involved burning birch bark near a solid surface, such as a stone. As the bark burned, tar vapors condensed against the cooler surface, leaving behind a sticky residue that could be collected.
These experiments allowed the scientists to investigate whether birch tar made through different prehistoric techniques would have similar antibacterial properties.
Prehistoric Birch Tar Shows Antibacterial Activity
The results revealed a potentially important benefit of this ancient material.
When the researchers tested their samples, every type of birch tar they produced was able to inhibit the growth of Staphylococcus aureus, a bacterium commonly associated with wound infections.
Staphylococcus aureus, often shortened to S. aureus, is particularly important in modern medicine because it can cause serious infections. Some strains have developed resistance to multiple antibiotics and are responsible for difficult-to-treat infections acquired in hospitals.
Remarkably, the antibacterial activity appeared regardless of which prehistoric extraction technique the researchers used. This suggests that the bacteria-inhibiting properties of birch tar were not dependent on one particular production method.
"The findings suggest that antimicrobial properties played a role as far back as the time of the early Neanderthals and could have been used in a targeted manner," explains Siemssen.
Although the experiments do not prove that Neanderthals actually applied birch tar to wounds, they demonstrate that the material they were capable of producing had properties that could have made it useful for medical care.
Could Neanderthal Medicine Offer Clues for Modern Antibiotics?
Beyond revealing another possible dimension of Neanderthal behavior, the discovery may also have implications for modern medicine.
Antibiotic resistance is a growing global health concern. As more bacteria become resistant to commonly used treatments, scientists are searching for additional substances that could help combat infections.
The antibacterial activity of prehistoric birch tar suggests that ancient materials and traditional medicinal practices may deserve closer scientific investigation. Substances used thousands of years ago could contain compounds with properties that remain relevant today.
However, the ability to inhibit bacteria in laboratory experiments does not necessarily mean that birch tar would be safe or effective as a treatment for human wounds. Further research would be needed to evaluate any potential medical applications.
"Our findings show that it might be worthwhile to examine targeted antibiotics from ethnographic contexts - or, as in this case, from prehistoric contexts - in greater depth," concludes Siemssen.
The findings add to a growing body of research portraying Neanderthals as resourceful humans who understood and exploited the natural materials around them. What archaeologists once regarded primarily as prehistoric glue may also have been a useful substance for protecting wounds, offering another intriguing possibility about the origins of human medical knowledge.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Cologne. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Tjaark Siemssen, Aderonke Oludare, Marcel Schemmel, Janos Puschmann, Matthias Bierenstiel. Antibacterial properties of experimentally produced birch tar and its medicinal affordances in the Pleistocene. PLOS One, 2026; 21 (3): e0343618 DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0343618

articles.title: Chinese pottery discovered in Great Zimbabwe reveals medieval African empire's vast connections spanning thousands of miles
articles.text:
Chinese pottery discovered in Great Zimbabwe reveals medieval African empire's vast connections spanning thousands of miles
Archaeologists excavating a medieval African kingdom have discovered pottery from eastern China, revealing connections across continents.
Archaeologists digging in the medieval city of Great Zimbabwe have discovered pieces of jade-green Chinese pottery, suggesting that the enigmatic empire had long-distance connections with East Asia more than 1,000 years ago.
Great Zimbabwe, located in the southeastern part of modern-day Zimbabwe, was the capital of an ancient empire that arose in southeastern Africa in around A.D. 1000. Little is known about this precolonial empire because its people did not leave a written history, but new archaeological excavations are shining a light on the enormous scale of the centuries-old civilization known for its intricate metalworking and ritual stone carvings.
In the new PBS documentary "Secrets of the Dead: Africa's Golden City," filmmakers followed a team of archaeologists from the field to the laboratory to try to answer questions surrounding the origins of the understudied civilization, its ritual and trade activities and why it disappeared after 500 years.
"When I was growing up, I was surrounded by symbols of Great Zimbabwe," University of Oxford archaeologist Shadreck Chirikure, who is leading the new excavations at the site, said in the documentary. "It was only when I started studying archaeology at university that I started realizing that there was this very big debate around who built Great Zimbabwe."
The site was first excavated in the late 19th century and quickly looted by British colonists for its ivory, metal and gold artifacts. These colonists insisted that Africans hadn't built Great Zimbabwe, instead claiming it arose from the Phoenicians, a people originally from the Mediterranean; they used that inaccuracy to justify taking all the artifacts to England, according to the documentary. Today, many Great Zimbabwean artifacts are held in the collection of the Pitt Rivers Museum at the University of Oxford.
But excavations are showing that Great Zimbabwe was a highly connected African kingdom that flourished from the 11th century until at least the 15th century, when the population may have gotten too large for the dry, over-farmed land to feed. Archaeologists have already discovered glass artifacts at Great Zimbabwe that came from Southeast Asia, India and the Middle East via boat.
"From India or Sri Lanka to Great Zimbabwe, it's at least 8,000 kilometers [5,000 miles]," Chirikure told Live Science. Merchants sailed the Indian Ocean using winds kicked up by monsoon cycles.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
"It's time we try to understand a bit more about trade and exchange," Chirikure said, "particularly by comparing the communities in places like Sri Lanka and southern Africa. Because it's the water that separated people, but it was also the water that connected people."
In this exclusive clip from the documentary, Chirikure and archaeologist Muchen Zhou, a doctoral student at the University of Oxford, examine a jade-green piece of pottery unearthed from the hillside at Great Zimbabwe. The glossy sheen on the sherd suggests the pot was fired at an extremely high temperature, a technological achievement that had only been accomplished in China at that early date. This style of pottery, called Longquan celadon, was made in eastern China starting around A.D. 950.
"We find it across the site of Great Zimbabwe," Chirikure said, but in small quantities. "This means the Chinese ceramics are a rarity. Perhaps they were used by the elites. They would have been quite a significant or highly valued exotic ware."
Other evidence of long-distance trade has been discovered at Great Zimbabwe, Chirikure said, including metal objects from what is today the Democratic Republic of Congo, around 1,250 miles (2,000 kilometers) away. The people of Great Zimbabwe were also sourcing copper and tin from modern-day South Africa, more than 300 miles (500 km) away. And chemical analysis of cattle bones has shown that some of the animals were being traded across an 87-mile (140 km) area.
RELATED STORIES
- Medieval Swahilis and Persians paired up 1,000 years ago in East Africa, ancient DNA reveals
- 'We do not know of a similar case': 4,000-year-old burial in little-known African kingdom mystifies archaeologists
- Ancient DNA from South Africa rock shelter reveals the same human population stayed there for 9,000 years
For his next project, Chirikure hopes to investigate local resources, such as soapstone, that hold a lot of meaning for the local Shona people, Zimbabwe's largest Indigenous group; and for Zimbabweans.
"Soapstone birds are an important part of Great Zimbabwe," he said, "but no one really knows where they got their soapstone from."
The Zimbabwe Bird, designed based on a series of birds carved from soapstone that were found at the archaeological site, is the national emblem and appears prominently on the country's flag.
"There are a number of soapstone outcrops around Great Zimbabwe," Chirikure said. "Next time in the field, that's one of the things I want to do — just go out there and try and find the geological sources of that soapstone."
The PBS documentary "Secrets of the Dead: Africa's Golden City" premieres Wednesday, Oct. 14, at 10 p.m. U.S. Eastern time.
Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

articles.title: Tòa nhà siêu thực mô phỏng "mật mã di truyền" của con người, tùy góc nhìn lại thấy nhiều hình dáng khác nhau
articles.text:
Một kiến trúc sư người Pháp ấp ủ hy vọng tạo ra các công trình tiết kiệm năng lượng và "ăn" khí CO2 đã chính thức thực hiện được giấc mơ này.
Theo CNN, kiến trúc sư Pháp khát khao chống lại hiện tượng Trái Đất ấm lên trên, ông Vincent Callebaut bộc bạch: "Tôi muốn đem hy vọng tới một ngày mai tốt đẹp hơn". Và ý tưởng của kiến trúc sư này đã được phát triển từ bản thiết kế trên giấy thành công trình lừng lững ngoài đời.
Thiết kế của tòa nhà Tao Zhu Yin Yuan.
Nằm ở quận Xinjin, trung tâm Đài Bắc, tòa nhà Tao Zhu Yin Yuan (Đào Chu Ẩn Viên) là một trung tâm thương mại tích hợp khách sạn và khu chung cư được rất nhiều người yêu thích ở Đài Loan bởi thiết kế vô cùng độc lạ. Tòa nhà này còn có nhiều tiện ích khác như câu lạc bộ, hồ bơi, phòng tập thể dục, sân đậu trực thăng trên mái…
Tòa nhà có hình dáng siêu thực này được thiết kế bởi Vincent Callebaut Architecture trên diện tích 42705 m², bắt đầu xây dựng vào năm 2013 và hoàn thành vào năm 2018 với 21 tầng, 42 căn hộ, cao 87m.
Tòa nhà Tao Zhu Yin Yuan có hình dáng siêu thực.
Nguyên mẫu thiết kế của tòa nhà Tao Zhu Yin Yuan là cấu trúc xoắn kép của phân tử DNA của con người, tạo nên một hình dáng độc đáo nổi bật khác hẳn với những công trình xung quanh.
Hệ thống cấu trúc của tòa nhà gồm lõi trung tâm hình trụ rất cứng với hai giàn leo ở tầng mái giống như một vận động viên trượt tuyết với lưng thẳng đứng và cánh tay mở rộng. Từ đó cung cấp một cốt lõi siêu nén chống động đất cực tốt và đem đến tính linh hoạt tối đa của các tầng nhà ở với khả năng hợp nhất hai đơn vị căn hộ thành một mà không cần một cầu nối nào.
Nguyên mẫu của tòa nhà là cấu trúc xoắn kép của phân tử DNA của con người.
Đặc biệt, mỗi tầng của tòa nhà được thiết kế quay 4,5 độ theo chiều kim đồng hồ so với tầng dưới và quay tổng cộng 90 độ qua 21 tầng, nên khi nhìn từ các góc độ khác nhau thì nó cũng biến đổi thành vô số hình dạng khác nhau như hình kim tự tháp, lúc là hình chữ thập, có khi là hình chóp ngược, hình elip và có lúc lại trông như hình trái tim khổng lồ…
Để đảm bảo mục tiêu thân thiện và tôn trọng môi trường, mọi không gian mở của tòa nhà như vườn ở tầng trệt, sân thượng và ban công của mỗi căn hộ đều được bao phủ bằng 23.000 cây xanh. Con số này cao hơn gần 5 lần so với quy định của địa phương, giúp hấp thụ khoảng 130 tấn carbon dioxide mỗi năm, khiến tòa nhà trở thành một công viên rừng đô thị đầy màu sắc.
Tòa nhà Tao Zhu Yin Yuan được bao phủ bởi nhiều cây xanh.
Ngoài ra, tòa nhà Tao Zhu Yin Yuan còn có một hệ thống chiếu sáng và thông gió tự nhiên. Mái nhà tích hợp pin mặt trời với diện tích bề mặt 1.000m² cung cấp điện năng được tạo ra từ tia mặt trời vào mạng lưới điện của tòa nhà. Nước mưa cũng được thu gom và tái chế từ trên mái để phục vụ sinh hoạt. Nhờ nguồn năng lượng thiên nhiên, tòa nhà đã giảm thêm 35 tấn lượng phát thải khí carbon dioxide mỗi năm.
Qua nhiều năm trời, kiến trúc sư Callebaut đã hoạt động năng nổ trong lĩnh vực công trình xanh, cho ra đời các thiết kế thân thiện với môi trường như vườn nổi giúp làm sạch các con sông tại châu Âu cho đến tòa nhà dưới nước có chất liệu là rác thải biển...

articles.title: Best wildlife cameras 2026: The ultimate buying guide to every major camera brand
articles.text:
Best wildlife cameras 2026: The ultimate buying guide to every major camera brand
A brand-by-brand guide to wildlife cameras, chosen for their autofocus capabilities, burst speed and animal tracking in real conditions, curated by our experts.
Wildlife photographers need a camera that is reliable and built to capture fast-moving action at a moment's notice. A fast burst rate, accurate autofocus and robust handling are vital when it comes to wildlife cameras, or you'll end up with sad, blurry photos of an empty tree stump.
We've curated a list of the best models from each of the top camera brands, so no matter which system you want to invest in, there will be something for you here.
Kimberley Lane, senior e-commerce writer for Live Science, has tested a wide range of optical equipment, including a huge variety of cameras and lenses. With over 7 years of photography experience, her skills span across many different genres, including landscape and seascape photography, wildlife, astrophotography and portrait work. Her photos have been featured in numerous national magazines, including Digital Camera World and Cosmopolitan.
Best Canon cameras for wildlife photography
Best for detail
Canon's highest-resolution mirrorless camera with a 45MP stacked sensor, the R5 II is for wildlife photographers who want a professional workflow and need to crop aggressively. It's flexible across multiple wildlife types and delivers pro-level output without going all the way up to the R1.
Read our full Canon EOS R5 II review
Pros
- 45.5MP resolution produces beautiful images and allows a lot of cropping room
- Stacked sensor enables faster readout speed, better noise handling and no rolling shutter
- 30FPS blackout-free burst rate is ideal for wildlife photography
- Excellent autofocus on moving subjects
- Chunky grip easily handles larger lenses
- Excellent hybrid shooter, boasting up to 8K 60p RAW video
Cons
- Only compatible with newer batteries
- Eye-control AF needs work
- Quite a bit more expensive than the new R6 III, which could be the more sensible option
Best intermediate
The new Canon EOS R6 III is an absolute triumph for wildlife photography, and it has solved all the niggles we had with the R6 II when we reviewed it. It has blackout-free 40FPS shooting and an improved 32.5MP sensor, with pre-continuous shooting and up to 7K video. This camera is hard to beat for enthusiasts and intermediate-level shooters.
Read our full Canon EOS R6 III review
Pros
- Blisteringly fast blackout-free 40FPS bursts
- Improved 32.5MP resolution compared to the Mark II's 24MP sensor.
- Pre-continuous shooting ensures you never miss a shot
- Sticky and accurate subject tracking (most of the time)
- Compatible with faster CFexpress cards
- Excellent battery life — we easily took over 6,000 images before our SD card gave out
- Beautiful color reproduction
Cons
- CFexpress card slot comes at the expense of a second SD card slot
- New LP-E6P battery means you'll have to invest in new spares
Best for pros
A monster camera for professional wildlife and sport photographers who need unrivaled power and reliability and can afford to invest in their photography career. Even though it doesn't have the best resolution, the stacked sensor produces less noise and better image quality, and allows for a faster readout speed.
Read the full Canon EOS R1 review at our sister site, Digital Camera World
Pros
- Stacked 24MP sensor
- Up to 40FPS blackout-free burst rate
- Intelligent AI autofocus
- Pre-continuous shooting to ensure you never miss a shot
- Built like a tank, with a large integrated vertical grip for professional sports and wildlife photography
- Dual CFexpress card slots
- 9.44 million dot viewfinder is bright and detailed
- Offers 6K video
Cons
- Not compatible with SD cards
- Not a small or lightweight camera — over 2.42 pounds (1.1kg) before you even add a lens
- 24MP resolution limits heavy cropping
- Very expensive
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
| Honorable mentions |  | 
|---|---|
| Canon EOS 90D | If you prefer a DSLR and are happy to stick with a hobbyist camera that won't receive any future updates. | 
| Canon EOS R7 | A beginner-friendly wildlife option with a 1.6x crop factor to extend the reach of your lenses — effectively a cheat code for wildlife photography. | 
| Canon EOS R6 II | If you like the look of the R6 III but want to save a bit of money, its predecessor is definitely still worthy of your hard-earned cash. | 
| Avoid: Canon EOS R8 | It's an excellent starter camera for more general styles, but the buffer fills up quickly and there aren't enough buttons and controls on the body to make it efficient for wildlife photography. | 
Best Sony cameras for wildlife photography
Best value for money
A big and welcome upgrade from the previous generation, with a new partially stacked sensor, improved AI autofocus and finally, a higher burst rate than the rather feeble 10FPS of the previous generation. The Sony A7 V is a very attractive option for wildlife, as well as general photography and hybrid shooting, but its Achilles heel is the shallow buffer, which fills up fast and will very quickly get annoying if you regularly shoot in bursts.
We will be reviewing the A7 V soon, but until then, you can read the full review at our sister site, Digital Camera World
Pros
- Blackout-free 30FPS burst rate with AF/AE tracking is much improved over the 10FPS in the previous model
- Features new partially stacked 33MP sensor to produce stunning and detailed images
- New AI subject detection can detect birds, animals and insects — including Eye AF
- This model now offers pre-capture, which captures images just before the shutter is pressed
- Handles noise well, which is an advantage if you're shooting at dawn or dusk, or are pairing it with a more affordable lens with an f/5.6 max aperture.
Cons
- Autofocus can struggle when shooting small birds or through foliage
- Buffer depth (~95 compressed RAW files) is shallow and will fill quickly
If you need heavy cropping power
With Sony's highest resolution yet, the monstrous A7R VI is the newest and most expensive model in the R lineup. Sony has finally answered our prayers by boosting the burst rate from 10FPS in the previous model up to a massive 30FPS in this new one. For this price, that's more like it. Plus, with a massive 67MP, you'll get some serious cropping power, which comes in handy if you're shooting distant wildlife or birds.
We will be reviewing the A7R VI soon, but for now, you can read the full review at our sister site, Digital Camera World
Pros
- Massive 67MP offers exceptional detail and leaves tons of room for cropping
- 30FPS blackout-free bursts seriously levels up the R range like never before
- Offers Continuous Shooting Speed Boost, which allows you to assign a custom button to temporarily jump from a lower, more sustained burst rate to the maximum 30FPS instantly, which avoids filling up the card too quickly
- AI subject detection has animal, bird and insect modes and is generally very accurate
- Pre-capture records images before you fully press the shutter
Cons
- Do you really need 67MP?
- High resolution means noisy images — we definitely found this to be the case with the previous generation
- Autofocus can be tripped up if your animal is partially covered by reeds or branches
- The most expensive release in the R range
Ultimate choice for pros
Experienced users looking for a balance of resolution and speed need look no further than the Sony A1 II. It has a 50.1MP stacked sensor, 30FPS bursts and Sony's class-leading AI autofocus, so what's not to love? That said, it's overkill for beginners and amateurs — plus we'd only recommend it if you can also invest in some of Sony's more expensive glass.
Read the full Sony A1 II review at our sister site, Digital Camera World
Pros
- A perfect blend of speed (30FPS blackout-free bursts) and resolution (50.1MP)
- Sticky, accurate AI autofocus with Eye AF for animals, birds and insects
- Both card slots accept CFexpress Type A or SD UHS-II/UHS-I
- RAW files offer incredible dynamic range
- Pre-capture starts taking images when the shutter is half-pressed
Cons
- Expensive, and will be wasted money unless you can also afford to invest in expensive lenses
- New Sony A7R VI is cheaper and has more resolution
- Overkill unless you're an experienced shooter
| Honorable mentions |  | 
|---|---|
| Sony A7R V | Stunning 61MP images, but with a much slower burst rate of 10FPS. It's long been our favorite Sony camera (until the new releases), and it's an excellent option if you don't shoot fast-moving animals or birds in flight. We've taken some beautiful wildlife images with it. | 
| Sony A7 IV | A more affordable option here, and it still has AI-powered autofocus, although the 33MP sensor isn't stacked like the new A7 V. Plus, like the previous generation R model, it only has a 10FPS burst rate. Still, its noise handling is excellent, and it is suitable for more general styles of photography. | 
| Sony A1 | If you don't need pre-capture, go for the original Sony A1. It's still a wildlife powerhouse with the same 50MP resolution and 30FPS bursts as the new Mark II. | 
| Sony A9 III | An absolute speed demon, but let's be honest — does anyone actually need 120FPS? Probably not. However, the Sony A9 III is considered to be one of the best cameras for birds in flight (BIF), but it'll be overkill unless you only shoot sports or fast-action bird photography. | 
| Avoid: older or entry-level Sony cameras | Sony's entry level and older cameras tend to be capped at around 10FPS burst rates, and the older models also don't have any AI-powered autofocus features, which make wildlife photography much more fruitful. It's a shame, as there's no real "beginner" Sony wildlife camera on the market that suits these criteria. | 
Best Nikon cameras for wildlife photography
The clear winner
For wildlife photography (and most other styles, too, while we're at it), the obvious choice for most Nikon shooters is the Nikon Z8. Often dubbed a "baby Z9", it has all the brains and brawn of the flagship Z9 in a smaller and more affordable package.
Read our full Nikon Z8 review
Pros
- 45.7MP resolution with a stacked sensor gives a lot of room for cropping
- Up to 120FPS bursts (11MP), or 20FPS sustained — all blackout-free
- Killer autofocus
- It can record more than 1,000 RAW images before any buffering kicks in — insanely useful for wildlife
- Performs well in low light
- Pre-release burst captures up to 1 second of images before the shutter is fully pressed
Cons
- Battery could be better
- 120FPS is only 11MP, which you likely won't need when you're buying a 45.7MP camera
- Occasional AF flaws
- Screen isn't fully articulating
If you need extra grip
If you saw the Z8 and thought, "Hey, I need something big and heavy", then the flagship R9 could be better for you. The integrated grip offers improved balance and weight distribution for longer lenses, although it's only compatible with CFexpress cards, making this model best suited for professionals.
Read the full Nikon Z9 review at our sister site, Digital Camera World
Pros
- Advanced 3D tracking and dedicated animal/bird eye AF
- Stunning 45.7MP resolution from a stacked sensor
- 20FPS blackout-free burst shooting for RAW images, with an option for 120FPS bursts at 11MP
- Pre-release burst can capture images up to 1 second before the shutter is fully pressed
- Robust, and built like a tank for heavy shooting over long periods
Cons
- Only compatible with expensive CFexpress cards
- Not as travel-friendly as the Z8 due to the bigger and heavier body
- Not many people will use 120FPS for 11MP images
- 3.69 million-dot EVF resolution is a little low compared to other flagship models like the Sony A1 II and Canon EOS R1 (9.44 million)
Best mid-range
For anyone on a moderate budget looking for a capable wildlife camera, the Nikon Z6 III has a partially stacked sensor, 20FPS RAW shooting and dedicated animal and bird detection modes, all wrapped up in a compact and lightweight body — the only downside being the rather limited 24.5MP resolution.
Read the full Nikon Z6 III review at our sister site, Digital Camera World
Pros
- 20FPS burst rate when shooting RAW images, up to 60FPS JPEG and up to 120FPS in DX crop mode.
- Partially-stacked sensor gives faster readout speed and reduced rolling shutter
- Clean images in low light
- Smaller and lighter than the Z8
- Bird detection added with a recent firmware update (2.0)
- Features pre-release capture to capture JPEG frames up to 1 second before fully releasing the shutter
Cons
- 24.5MP resolution won't allow for heavy cropping
- Some users report that the autofocus struggles with birds in flight at a distance
- Pre-release capture doesn't yet support RAW files
| Honorable mentions |  |

| Nikon D850 | Known as one of the best DSLRs ever made, the Nikon D850 is an incredible choice if you don't need the bells and whistles of a mirrorless — but keep in mind that it won't receive any future updates. | 
| Nikon CoolPix P1000 | If you need unparalleled zoom, the P1000 bridge camera has an insane 24-3,000mm zoom range. There are drawbacks, including the limited 16MP resolution and lack of weather sealing, but for beginners who want an all-in-one package for casual shooting, it's definitely worth a look. | 
| Nikon D500 | An affordable, entry-level APS-C model with 10FPS bursts, sharp 20MP images and fierce autofocus. | 
| Avoid: Older DSLRs | Older DSLR models are typically much slower, have outdated autofocus and limited ISO performance for low-light work. | 
Best OM System cameras for wildlife photography
Best overall
Wildlife photographers who want a powerful system in a small package should look at the OM-1 Mark II — it can shoot a blisteringly fast 50FPS with full AF/AE tracking (or 120FPS with locked focus), and even though the 20.4MP resolution sounds a little on the low side, we were pleasantly surprised by the image quality.
Read our full OM System OM-1 Mark II review
Pros
- Insane 120FPS burst rate with locked focus, up to 50FPS with AF/AE tracking
- Surprisingly good images for 20.4MP
- Accurate autofocus with bird and human modes
- Compact and lightweight, even when paired with long lenses
- Pro Capture captures images before shutter is fully pressed
- Buffer can hold around 213 RAW frames at 120FPS
Cons
- 20.4MP may be underwhelming for some users, and doesn't allow for heavy cropping
- Not enough of an upgrade if you already own the OM-1
- Noisy low-light images

For hobbyists
If you're just getting into wildlife photography and don't need the best of the best, the OM-5 Mark II is a great camera for people who want to photograph wildlife among other styles. It lacks dedicated bird/animal subject detection, but on the whole, OM System's autofocus is still pretty good.
Read the full OM-5 Mark II review at our sister site, Digital Camera World

- The small grip might make it more difficult to hold it with larger lenses
For something more robust
While MFT cameras are often favored for being small and lightweight, big lenses can often feel unbalanced. The OM-D E-M1X fixes this issue with its integrated vertical grip, and the speedy bursts and AI animal detection modes are ideal for fast action — we called it a "wildlife wonder."

Best Fujifilm cameras for wildlife photography
The action specialist
With its speedy burst shooting, accurate autofocus and stacked sensor, the X-H2S is ideal for fast action shooting, birds in flight and hybrid photo/video shooters.

Versatile high-res
The Fuji X-T5 is a compact APS-C camera to suit traveling photographers perfectly, but the small buffer and hit-and-miss autofocus are better suited to photographing slow-moving, larger mammals as opposed to fast action and birds. Best Panasonic cameras for wildlife photography
Best for fast-moving wildlife

Read the full Panasonic Lumix G9 II review at our sister site, Digital Camera World
Pros
- Up to 60FPS bursts with continuous autofocus
- Micro Four Thirds sensor gives extra reach with 2x crop factor — and allows for more compact lenses
- Pre-capture records up to 1.5 seconds before the shutter is fully released
