articles.title: Floqer's AI agents research sales prospects so teams don't have to | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Floqer is an autonomous customer knowledge platform that provides business-to-business sales and marketing teams with an AI-powered database designed to continuously collect, organize, and update the information used to understand their customers.
Floqer is pitching Wednesday on the Startup Battlefield stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026. The startup told TechCrunch ahead of the presentation that it plans to open-source the technology behind its autonomous customer knowledge database. It’s targeting early 2027 for the release, pending security reviews.
Floqer also says it has surpassed $1.2 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR), and that its overall revenue has grown roughly tenfold over the past year.
The startup was founded by Shivam Mahajan, the CEO, and Zaaheda Islam, who met at university. Before Floqer, Mahajan worked as a software engineer at Kyndryl, and Islam worked as a senior data scientist at Axis Capital.
Floqer’s first product looked nothing like its current one. “We started with a Chrome extension, which is called ‘Super Chat,’” Mahajan told TechCrunch in an interview earlier this month. “Anybody can go and log in with their ChatGPT account and then understand [information] and take notes.”
The founders soon noticed that enterprise companies were using the extension to clean up data in their customer relationship management (CRM) systems. Conversations with those companies showed that keeping CRM data clean was mostly manual work, with few established processes for keeping customer records up to date.
“When we spoke with them, they told us that it’s super manual for them to clean their CRM data, and there were no established processes around that,” Mahajan said. “So that was insightful for us, and then we pivoted from there to build Floqer.”
The problem Floqer is trying to solve is familiar to anyone who has worked in sales or revenue operations. Finding potential customers takes hours of searching Google, LinkedIn, company websites, job boards, and other sources to identify companies that fit a particular profile, then tracking down the right people and their contact information.
Floqer aims to automate much of that research. Users can describe what they are looking for, and its AI agents search across different sources to build lists of relevant companies and contacts.
The company says its system can enrich accounts, or add detail about the companies a sales team is targeting, using more than 100 third-party data sources. When it needs a verified email address or phone number, Floqer uses a “waterfall” approach, checking one data provider after another until it finds usable information.
The system also continuously monitors the web for changes. If a prospect changes jobs, gets promoted, or works at a company that raises new funding, those updates can be reflected in the user’s customer records.
Floqer describes the technology as a fleet of AI agents that continuously research companies, people, and customer interactions, so team members don’t have to perform that work manually. According to the company, customers have reported cutting prospecting time by as much as 70%.
“Our autonomous customer knowledge database is only available to a limited audience, mostly due to how much demand our team can actually serve properly,” Mahajan said. “But open-sourcing it will help us fix that.”
The decision comes partly in response to customer demand. Mahajan said some companies want to host their own data rather than keep it inside a vendor’s proprietary platform. Others want to modify the technology or build on top of it.
“Our mission is to really enable every team to build their central source of growth,” Mahajan said.
Before releasing the database publicly, Floqer is conducting security reviews because the database can contain sensitive customer information and large companies already use it.
Floqer was founded in 2024 and has raised $2 million in pre-seed funding, with participation from investors such as Perplexity’s F7 Fund, N49P, Tidal Venture Partners, and Perplexity co-founder Denis Yarats. It says it now has eight employees and more than 1,000 customers, including Perplexity, Wise, and AngelList.

articles.title: Apple’s new HomeView smart display is $10 cheaper at Amazon
articles.text:
Apple only just announced on Tuesday that its first smart display, the HomeView, will arrive on November 13th, but you can already save a couple bucks on it. Right now, you can buy the display for $289.99 ($10 off) in gray and the creamy white “starlight” colorway at Amazon. Sure, it’s a small discount, but deals on new Apple devices ahead of launch are rare.
Apple’s new HomeView smart display is $10 cheaper at Amazon
Apple’s first smart display doesn’t arrive until November 13th, but you can save on a couple of colorways.
Expect a full review of the HomeView in November, but my colleague Jennifer Pattison Tuohy spent some brief time with it and likened it to an “iPhone for your home” that looks a bit like an oversized Apple Watch. It features a gorgeous seven-inch square touchscreen that can recognize up to six household members and automatically switch between personalized experiences, displaying information relevant to whoever is using it.
As you might already know, the HomeView also doubles as a smart home hub, with support for Matter and Thread. You can use it to control compatible smart home devices, view live feeds and recorded footage from HomeKit Secure Video cameras, and more. It also features a 12-megapixel FaceTime camera for video calls, and doubles as an entertainment device, letting you play music, display photos, and more.
Apple’s AI-powered Siri assistant is another big part of the experience, allowing you to ask questions and get information using personal context from your messages, calendar, and emails. That means you can ask it to find your lost keys, play a song someone texted you, pull up a recipe with step-by-step instructions and built-in timers, or help you keep track of your schedule without having to reach for your phone.

articles.title: Netflix to lay off 1,000 staff amid intensifying competition for user attention | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Netflix is laying off about 6% of its employee base, or close to 1,000 staff, the company confirmed to TechCrunch.
The streaming giant said most of the cuts would affect its product, tech, legal, and human resources departments. The company said it will “continue to invest aggressively in high impact areas” to improve its service, and stated it is on track to deliver its full-year forecast.
Netflix had 16,000 full-time employees as of the end of last year, according to its annual filing with regulators.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the news, citing an internal memo sent to employees.
“Our mission—to entertain the world—is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources,” the Journal cited the company’s co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters as writing in the memo.
The layoffs come in the wake of a protracted bidding war for Warner Bros. Discovery’s streaming and studio businesses that Netflix lost to Paramount Skydance earlier this year. Netflix ostensibly saw great potential in Warner Bros.’ assets, which include its studios, HBO, streaming platforms, games, and TV networks such as CNN and HGTV.
Long the dominant TV app, Netflix has in recent years faced intensifying competition from the likes of YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, and other social apps to attract and keep users’ eyes. According to reports from various market research firms, social apps like TikTok are catching up to Netflix when it comes to user engagement, and YouTube is said to have surpassed Netflix in average daily viewing in 2025.
The streaming giant has been trying extensively to extract more value from its subscribers, raising prices, expanding its ad-supported tier, and investing in live events and sports, gaming, and children’s programming to increase user engagement.
It has also bet on AI-supported features, gaming, and video podcasts, and has dabbled in short-form video content alongside redesigning its mobile app to compete for users’ attention with social media platforms.
In 2025, Netflix reported revenue of $45.2 billion, and said ad revenue had risen to over $1.5 billion.

articles.title: Humanly acquires CareerArc, adding recruitment marketing to its AI hiring tools
articles.text:
Humanly has acquired recruitment marketing company CareerArc, its fifth acquisition since 2025, with no price disclosed. The AI hiring tools it is consolidating fall into the EU AI Act’s high-risk employment category, whose duties were delayed to December 2027.
Humanly has bought CareerArc, its fifth acquisition in two years. No price was disclosed, and the buyer employs 50 people.
The deal pairs Humanly’s automated chat, screening and interview tools with CareerArc’s social recruiting software and interactive career-site maps, GeekWire reported.
Humanly is based in Bellevue, Washington, and was founded in 2018. CareerArc dates to 2009 and sits in Burbank, California.
Nine of CareerArc’s 13 staff are joining. Humanly bought Sprockets, Qualifi and HourWork in 2025, and the employee engagement platform Anthill earlier this year.
It has raised $52M in total, including $25M in April, and counts Microsoft, Domino’s and MGM Resorts among more than 120 customers.
What it is assembling is a category European law treats separately. Annex III of the AI Act makes AI used for recruitment and selection high-risk, including screening applications and evaluating candidates.
Those duties were pushed to December 2027 by the Omnibus, from August this year, alongside six other categories.
One obligation did not move. The AI Act’s transparency rules took effect on 2 August and apply whether or not a system is high-risk, which reaches candidate-facing chat of the kind Humanly sells.
European employers are the most reluctant buyers. A Morgan McKinley survey found more than half of UK employers do not use AI to hire, against 36% across seven markets.
Candidates are warier still. Some 23% said being assessed by AI would make them far less likely to apply, rising to 28% in the UK, and only 5% would accept a decision made by AI alone. Another 44% would accept one with a human involved.
London has its own entry. Ethos raised $22.75M from Andreessen Horowitz to match experts to work, and lists possible high-risk classification under the AI Act among its own risks.
The consolidation logic is volume. Humanly sells to high-volume employers, and a quarter of employers in the same survey said rising application numbers are slowing their screening. Generative AI is part of why, with 78% of jobseekers in that survey using it to look for work.
What the deal does not come with is a number. There is no price, no revenue figure, and nothing on how many of the five acquired products survive as products.

articles.title: Jim Cramer explains why even strong bank earnings couldn't save their stocks
articles.text:
The nation's biggest banks delivered mixed third-quarter results this week, but Wall Street's reaction was overwhelmingly negative, with all six major bank stocks falling despite some strong results.
CNBC's Jim Cramer said Wednesday, on Day 2 of the financial earnings flood, that investors appear more concerned about what lies ahead than what the banks just reported.
"Frankly, it's strange to see such universally negative reactions to a set of quarters that contained plenty of positives," the "Mad Money" host said. "But this is what happens when investors are worried about the future, and it's hard not to worry with persistent inflation, rising interest rates, and newly wobbly capital markets."
Here's what stood out from each bank's report.
Wells Fargo
Wells Fargo reported a mixed quarter Tuesday, beating earnings estimates but falling short on revenue. Net interest margin — a key profitability gauge, measuring the spread between what a bank earns on loans and pays out on deposits — stabilized at 2.43%, slightly ahead of expectations. That stabilization was particularly encouraging after the bank had missed net interest margin estimates in nine of the previous 10 quarters. Shares fell following the report, but Cramer's Charitable Trust, the portfolio used by the CNBC Investing Club, upgraded the stock to a buy-equivalent rating. "CEO Charlie Scharf emphasized that his bank is set up to do much better in a higher interest rate environment and, given his track record, I believe him," Cramer said. Wells Fargo stock rose slightly Wednesday.
JPMorgan Chase
JPMorgan Chase missed expectations on both the top and bottom lines on Tuesday. Weakness in fixed income trading and asset management weighed on results, while expenses rose faster than revenue. On the earnings call, though, management offered better-than-expected net interest income forecasts for the fourth quarter and 2027. The stock initially struggled but recovered much of its losses as investors digested the outlook. For Cramer, the quarter "wasn't much of a needle-mover for the world's largest bank." JPMorgan stock gained nearly 1% in Wednesday's awful market.
Citigroup
Citigroup delivered one of the stronger headline reports on Tuesday. Revenue grew 8% year over year, marking the bank's best third-quarter performance in a decade, while management raised its full-year net interest income outlook. Citi also stood out as the only major bank to exceed fixed-income trading revenue expectations. Despite those positives, shares tumbled 5.6% following the report. "My suspicion is that Citi's stock was punished for its recent outperformance," Cramer said. "Before yesterday's beatdown, it was running circles around the rest of the group. But if you believe in the turnaround, as I do, this is a buying opportunity." Citi shares dropped another 1.8% on Wednesday.
Bank of America
On Wednesday, Bank of America delivered one of the most disappointing reports of the group, missing revenue and earnings expectations while also contending with a $1.2 billion regulatory penalty tied to alleged violations of anti-money-laundering and sanctions laws. The bank's capital markets businesses were particularly weak, with investment banking fees declining 11% and fixed-income trading revenue falling 17%. Although management highlighted continued growth in deposits and lending, those positives weren't enough to offset the disappointing results. Shares fell roughly 5% following the print.
Goldman Sachs
Goldman Sachs "put up some excellent numbers" Tuesday, comfortably beating top and bottom line estimates. Investment banking fees rose 21%, while equities trading revenue surged 72%, offsetting weaker-than-expected fixed-income trading. Management also struck an optimistic tone, highlighting opportunities to finance the AI infrastructure buildout and a robust investment banking backlog. Yet shares surrendered an early rally and finished Tuesday slightly lower. "When a company reports such strong numbers and the stock gets slammed anyway, that tells you there are a lot of skeptics out there," he said. "They think the boom times are over. I don't agree, but that's the market's verdict, at least for the moment." Cramer's Charitable Trust upgraded Goldman to a buy-equivalent rating following the report, viewing the pullback as a buying opportunity. The stock lost another 1.5% on Wednesday.
Morgan Stanley
Morgan Stanley also topped expectations on Wednesday. The bank's Institutional Securities Group, which houses its investment banking and sales and trading segments, saw revenue rise 18%, while wealth management revenue grew 10%. CEO Ted Pick said that he was "cautiously optimistic about the fourth quarter," with the bank reportedly positioned to lead Anthropic's anticipated IPO. Still, shares fell almost 3% despite the solid results, reflecting investors' reluctance to reward even better-than-expected earnings amid broader concerns about the banking sector.

articles.title: Jim Cramer says don't give up on this unpredictable market. Here's why
articles.text:
While strong earnings were not enough to rescue stocks in this unpredictable market, CNBC's Jim Cramer warned on Wednesday that investors who give up now could miss out on the next rally.
Stocks tumbled on the session, with the S&P 500 down just over 1%, the Nasdaq shedding 1.9% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average closing slightly lower.
Cramer said that uncertainty surrounding inflation, interest rates and the war with Iran makes it nearly impossible to anticipate the market's next move. "You just want to throw things away and go home," the "Mad Money" host added. "If you do, though, will you be able to buy them back in time for those 10 days of the year where all the gains are made? I don't think so."
Historical market data underscores that risk. According to JPMorgan, an investor who put $10,000 into the S&P 500 and missed its 10 best trading days between 2005 and 2024 would have ended up with less than half the wealth of someone who stayed fully invested.
Cramer pointed to Wednesday's inflation report as an example of the market's unpredictability. Consumer prices rose 0.6% in September from the previous month, slightly more than expected, initially sending Treasury yields higher. They later reversed course, even as oil prices continued climbing. Typically, hotter inflation pushes yields higher as investors anticipate more aggressive interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve.
The conflicting signals have complicated the expectations game regarding the Federal Reserve's next move. Another rate hike could slow the economy, while holding rates steady risks pushing long-term borrowing costs higher. Cramer argued that an end to the war with Iran could send oil prices sharply lower, easing inflation without further Fed intervention.
Corporate earnings have offered little clarity. Investment bank Morgan Stanley reported a decent quarter, but shares still fell nearly 3%. Similarly, semiconductor equipment maker ASML reported strong earnings and growing demand, only to see its stock reverse early gains and close down 4% alongside the broader chip sector rout.
With economic data and corporate results failing to provide clear direction, he said that "it becomes very hard to have conviction." Still, he cautioned against abandoning stocks altogether. Even investors who successfully avoid further losses risk missing the market's eventual recovery.

articles.title: S&P 500 futures fall as traders await more U.S. economic data: Live updates
articles.text:
Futures tied to the S&P 500 slid on Wednesday night, with traders looking ahead to more earnings reports and economic data following a losing session brought about by hotter-than-expected inflation data.
S&P 500 futures slipped 0.2%, while Nasdaq-100 futures dropped 0.7%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures rose just 22 points.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite shed 1.9% during regular trading, marking its worst day since July 23 — when it dropped 2.2%. The S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, its biggest one one-day slide since July 29. The Dow was the relative outperformer, falling just 0.1%.
In Asia, futures for Hong Kong's Hang Seng index stood at 24,074 lower than the index's last close of 24,314.17. Japan's Nikkei 225 was also set to fall at open, with its Chicago futures at 66,225, compared with the index's previous close of 67,744.29. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was down 0.85% in its first hour of trade.
There are growing concerns that the Federal Reserve could tighten monetary policy more aggressively before year-end, after new data showed consumer prices in September rose faster than expected on a year-over-year basis.
"Inflation is cooking with gas," said Jamie Cox, managing partner for Harris Financial Group. "It is abundantly clear where the inflation impulse originates, but two wars need to end before we get any relief. The Federal Reserve made the mistake of calling Covid era inflation transitory, and now it appears they are set to make the same mistake in reverse on the energy supply shock."
Investors will get even more inflation data on Thursday, with the September reading on producer prices due out at 8:30 a.m. ET. New retail sales figures and weekly jobless claims are also slated for release at that time.
The corporate earnings season continues as well, with regional banks U.S. Bancorp and PNC due to report. Charles Schwab is also scheduled to post earnings.

articles.title: OpenAI sued by 8 states over ChatGPT safety concerns
articles.text:
Eight states filed lawsuits against OpenAI on Wednesday alleging that the artificial intelligence company's ChatGPT chatbot is an unsafe product that's harmed children and deceived parents.
Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana have individually sued OpenAI in their own state courts, Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a release. She said Iowa's lawsuit aims to "vindicate the rights of Iowans affected by OpenAI's willful, dangerous, reckless, and unlawful conduct."
"OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans," Bird said in a statement. "OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it's giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide — all while pretending to be their fake friend. My lawsuit is about protecting our kids and holding OpenAI accountable under our state law."
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company has built age-specific protections into its product that "many other AI products lack." He added that OpenAI is working with states to advance policies that will apply to the entire industry.
"While no system can be perfect, we'll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today," Pusateri said.
OpenAI is facing mounting scrutiny over its safety and security practices, including around how the company is working to protect children. In a number of wrongful death lawsuits, ChatGPT is blamed for driving users to experience harmful delusions and, in some cases, to commit suicide. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier also sued OpenAI in June, alleging the company knowingly released an unsafe product that could harm users.
OpenAI has taken steps to enhance safety features for parents and children over the last year, and in August it launched a dedicated experience for minors called ChatGPT for Teens. That product includes a range of educational features and age-appropriate safeguards that are intended to reduce exposure to developmentally inappropriate or harmful content.
"Teens should be able to use AI to learn, create, and explore," OpenAI said in a release at the time. "But that access should come with protections that reflect their developmental stage, reinforce real-world relationships, and support healthy use over time."
If you are having suicidal thoughts or are in distress, contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 for support and assistance from a trained counselor.

articles.title: OpenAI bugging suspect booked one-way ticket to Saudi Arabia with family before arrest
articles.text:
Abdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi national charged with secretly installing a recording device in an executive conference room at OpenAI, had booked a one-way ticket from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia with his wife and a third family member before his arrest, federal prosecutors told a judge in a newly unsealed court filing.
Alfozan "has the means — and will have the incentive — to flee the United States sooner if he learns about this case before he is arrested," the U.S. Attorney's Office in San Francisco said in the Oct. 8 filing, which asked a judge to seal a criminal complaint against him and a warrant for his arrest.
The filing said the tickets were booked for Oct. 12, from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia via Istanbul.
The judge granted the sealing request, and Alfozan was arrested Oct. 9, the Department of Justice has said.
He has been detained since his arrest.
Alfozan, 35, is a venture partner in a Saudi Arabian venture capital firm that lists a prince from that nation's ruling royal family as a fellow partner.
The VC firm, Raed Ventures, says on its website that Alfozan, who lives in the San Francisco area, "is a seasoned technology professional with deep experience in startups, entrepreneurship, and scaling tech companies."
"He currently serves as Engineering Lead at OpenAI, with a focus on AI Agents and the data platform," Alfozan's bio page on Raed's site says.
Raed, which focuses on investments in the Middle East, announced Alfozan had joined the firm on Feb. 8, 2025, two days after Raed said Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud had joined as a venture partner. A venture partner usually is a consulting or project-based role, not an investing partner or director who is responsible for raising funds or leading deals.
Alfozan had worked at OpenAI since July 2025, according to the Department of Justice. The company said it terminated him this month.
The Financial Times reported Wednesday that when Saudi tech influencers visited San Francisco in September, "it was Alfozan who welcomed them to OpenAI offices where he gave them tours."
A former CIA official with extensive experience in the Middle East, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the nature of their past work, told CNBC that Raed Ventures is "basically a state organ" of the Saudi government. One of Raed's funds in December 2024 received an investment from Saudi Venture Capital, a subsidiary of SME Bank, which is part of Saudi Arabia's National Development Fund.
In addition to being a venture partner in Raed, the prince, Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud, is a member of the ruling Al Saud family, and the managing director and vice chairman of his family's private office, according to his bio on Raed's website.
The former CIA official said that if Alfozan's alleged bugging of OpenAI is part of a state-sponsored espionage effort, it shows that "in the AI and tech boom, even the kingdom of Saudi Arabia has assessed that the risk is worth the gain to engage in economic espionage against a close ally."
The former official also said this incident is "probably the tip of the iceberg."
The criminal complaint against Alfozan does not allege that Raed or its other partners were aware of Alfozan allegedly planting a recording device at OpenAI.
The case is being prosecuted by the National Security, Cyber & Special Prosecutions Section of the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California, according to the Department of Justice.
Alfozan is charged in U.S. District Court in San Francisco with one count of using or attempting to use an electronic, mechanical or other device to intercept oral communications.
He is being detained pending an Oct. 19 detention hearing, where his lawyer could argue for his release on bond. If convicted, he faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, DOJ said.
Alfozan is not charged with corporate espionage or stealing trade secrets.
OpenAI earlier this year held discussions with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, the country's sovereign wealth fund, about investing in the AI company.
Raed did not immediately respond to requests for comment. CNBC has also requested comment from the Saudi embassy in Washington.
Alfozan's criminal defense attorney, William Pernik, told CNBC by email, "At this point, the information provided has been extremely limited, as the charging documents have just been unsealed yesterday."
OpenAI declined to comment on Wednesday about whether it knew about Alfozan's position at the Saudi firm. And the company said it can't share more details about the conference room in question due to operational security concerns.
The company said in a post on X on Tuesday, "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."
"We take protecting our technology, data and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance,"
the company said. "Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats."
Alfozan, in a recent interview with the podcast Identity Capital about his career, noted that in July 2016, he and other Saudi nationals who were working at various tech companies in Silicon Valley met with their nation's now-de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. The prince was visiting Silicon Valley as part of a U.S. tour to promote his "Vision 2030" economic diversification plan.
"One of the issues we discussed was whether we should move back to [the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia] now and bring our technical skills to improve the economy ... or should we work a few more years before we go back in order to gain more experience," Alfozan said in the interview, which was conducted in Arabic, translated by CNBC and posted online Sept. 24.
Bin Salman replied that "the country was undergoing major development and did not have the talent to train the next generation who would carry on those development plans," Alfozan said.
Alfozan added that the group of young workers "decided it was best to continue to learn and develop our skills before taking our knowledge back to [Saudi Arabia] to improve the tech sector."
Throughout the podcast, Alfozan discusses in detail his trajectory from coding in high school in Dammam, Saudi Arabia, to his career in the U.S. At one point in the interview, he refers to himself as an "introvert," who still pushes himself to help other young professionals find success in Silicon Valley.
Days after the podcast was posted, on Sept. 30, a federal criminal complaint alleges that OpenAI staff discovered "a surreptitious audio recording device inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in" a conference room.
The device, which had a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage, was concealed in toilet paper, according to the complaint.
Alfozan had no authority to enter the conference room, which is frequently used for "discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information," according to the complaint.
The conference room can be reserved "only by executives and executive assistants," and is typically used "for internal leadership meetings and technical and product sessions, as well as external briefings with government officials and business counterparts," the complaint said.
Closed-circuit TV footage at OpenAI showed Alfozan close to the conference room on multiple days in September at various times, according to the complaint.
The filing also said that in August, and again in September, Alfozan used an AI productivity tool to inquire about OpenAI's building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, as well as "external partner meetings."
And a chatbot associated with Alfozan's spouse, which the complaint alleges shared several identifying characteristics with his own account, allegedly submitted detailed prompts about building, customizing, installing and remotely accessing a recording device. Alfozan's spouse, who was not identified in the complaint, has not been charged with any wrongdoing.
After the recording device was found hidden in the TV in the conference room, OpenAI placed a camera in that room, the complaint says.
Alfozan was seen on that camera entering the conference room at about 1:20 p.m. on Oct. 5, and "checking behind the television into which Recording Device 1 had been inserted," the complaint alleges.
That same day, the complaint said, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a printer room at OpenAI.
Inside that bag, OpenAI security found his wallet, ID and "another recording device" made by the same Chinese manufacturer, Seeed, which made the device found inserted in the conference room's TV, the complaint says.
The second recording device, like the first one, "had a recording microcontroller," and "had been customized to obfuscate anything stored on the device, such as potentially intercepted audio communications," the complaint said.
Alfozan reported to OpenAI that he had lost the bag, which was returned to him without the second recording device, according to the complaint. He did not inquire about the device, although he asked about certain other items that he said were missing, the complaint said.
"Any attempt to illicitly obtain protected information from U.S. super intelligence and technology companies threatens both American innovation and the national security interests those advancements support," Scott Schelble, special agent in charge of the FBI San Francisco Field Office, said in a statement on Tuesday about Alfozan's arrest, using the Trump administration's preferred term for artificial intelligence.
Before joining OpenAI, Alfozan had a long track record of work experience in the Bay Area.
On his LinkedIn page, Alfozan describes himself as an "Experienced Engineering Lead with 11 years of building scalable and reliable software systems in the data and AI/ML domains."
"Proven track record of leading engineering teams, delivering complex projects and enterprise products. 
Driven by strong project management skills and a passion for cultivating a culture of collaboration and engineering excellence," his bio there says.
Before joining OpenAI, Alfozan was a founding engineer at Nash, an AI firm focused on logistics, according to his LinkedIn page.
And prior to Nash, he worked as a senior systems engineer at Facebook's parent company, Meta, from 2017 through 2022, according to his LinkedIn page. His internships before that included one at Microsoft in 2014, his bio says.
Alfozan studied computer science and engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and data science at the University of California, Berkeley, according to his LinkedIn page.
MIT's media relations office said he was enrolled there from January 2011 through January 2014, and again from February 2016 through May 2016, without receiving a degree.
A UC Berkeley spokesperson said Alfozan attended the school from January 2023 through May 2025, and earned a master's degree.
In 2016, he was a research intern at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology in Saudi Arabia, he said on LinkedIn.
In 2020, he won a $50,000 second prize in the Saudi Covid-19 Challenge, a hackathon event, according to the profile.
Alfozan's home, on a hill in Millbrae, California, overlooks San Francisco Bay with views of Mount Diablo. The small San Mateo County suburb, which is popular with tech workers, is located about 30 minutes south of San Francisco and 25 minutes from Stanford University. No one answered the doorbell of the home Wednesday when a CNBC reporter rang.
The Financial Times reported that Alfozan was "born in the ultraconservative central region of Qassim," but "grew up in Dammam in the kingdom's oil-rich Eastern Province."
The FT also reported that in a documentary about Alfozan that aired on Saudi television, his father said that as a young student in a government-backed program for gifted children to develop skills in mathematics, physics and engineering, Alfozan "would read the encyclopedia cover to cover."
"We are waiting to see what evidence the government has against our client, and look forward to presenting all appropriate defenses in court," Pernik, Alfozan's attorney, said.
"What I can tell you by way of a statement is that, like countless Americans, Mr. Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream," the attorney said. "He spent years studying, working and contributing to an American technological sector that leads the world, a sector built in large part by immigrants like him."
"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible, and any possible reasons why," Pernik said.
The lawyer noted that Alfozan is "charged with violating a federal recording statute, not stealing trade secrets or working as a foreign agent."
"There is no evidence to suggest otherwise at this time that has been shared with us," Pernik said. "Where someone was born is not evidence of anything and national origins is — and always should be — a protected status under our system of laws."
— Ashley Capoot, Lora Kolodny and Reem Nasr contributed to this report.

articles.title: Dell stock plunges 11%, leading data center sell-off as fears mount about 'enterprise AI timing'
articles.text:
Dell shares plummeted 11% on Wednesday and dragged down other data center equipment names on mounting concerns that enterprise spending on artificial intelligence won't justify the AI buildout.
Hewlett-Packard Enterprise, Oracle and Super Micro all joined in the downward slide.
In a report to clients on Wednesday, analysts at Barclays downgraded its rating on Dell, HPE and NetApp, "after a significant run and on enterprise AI timing."
Makers of data center servers and other backend equipment have been favored on Wall Street this year on optimism that they'll be selling huge volumes of gear tied to demand for AI chips and systems for years into the future. Dell has been one of the top performers on the market, up more than 300% this year, while HPE has jumped about 160% and NetApp has doubled.
However, sentiment toward the AI infrastructure space has shifted of late due in part to concerning revenue figures out of OpenAI and more broadly out of fear that rising interest rates will create a challenging environment as so much of the buildout is reliant on debt. Oracle, a heavy borrower, dropped 9% on Wednesday and is now down 33% for the year while neocloud CoreWeave plunged 15%, wiping out its gains for 2026.
The Barclays analysts said they haven't seen a "meaningful AI inflection" when it comes to enterprise spending for Dell, HPE and NetApp, lowering the rating on each to the equivalent of a hold from buy. They instead attribute increased revenue to the global memory shortage and noted that infrastructure companies have passed the higher price of memory along to customers.
"There is growing sentiment about enterprise AI adoption creating a hardware refresh," the Barclays analysts wrote, adding that businesses are typically allocating just 5% of their IT budgets to AI. "We believe the strong enterprise revenues are more of a function of memory costs than a move to enterprise AI at this time."
The Barclays analysts also found that only about a quarter of total enterprise AI spend is going towards hardware. They said normalizing and eventually declining memory prices could weigh on infrastructure-related revenue.
Memory is a notoriously cyclical business, and stocks were hit this week after China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, reported progress over the weekend on a new chip structure. Micron is down 11% for the week, while South Korea's SK Hynix has tumbled 13% in U.S. trading and Western Digital has dropped more than 8%.
WATCH: HPE isn’t Dell, but its lower valuation gives it more upside, says Jim Cramer

articles.title: Microsoft's wild ride back to record highs in 1 chart — and the lessons learned
articles.text: Microsoft has climbed back to record highs after a turbulent year for the tech giant's stock. Those who held on should briefly enjoy the view — and then find lessons from the rocky ride to make money again in the future. Before Tuesday, it had been almost a year since Microsoft last closed at a record: Oct. 28, 2025, at $542.07 a share. The next evening, Microsoft signaled that its spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure would accelerate in the coming quarters, sending shares down about 3% in response. In that moment, it was impossible for investors to know what awaited them: a brutal, monthslong decline that saw shares lose more than one-third of their value, driven in part by some existential questions about the company's future in an AI-first world. Fast forward to present, and like a phoenix rising from the ashes, Microsoft has rallied back to secure its first record close in nearly 12 months, ending Tuesday's session at $543.45. Though it pulled back nearly 2% Wednesday in a terrible market, the journey here is no less remarkable. It's easy to sit back and say, "Of course, we knew it would come back." But victory laps aren't what make you a better investor. On the other hand, a diligent study of the dynamics that got the stock back here can do that. There are lessons we can pull from this experience that we will carry forward with us. What went wrong This time last year, Microsoft was basically sitting on top of the world. It had a stake in OpenAI that seemed to get more valuable by the week . The AI infrastructure buildout wasn't a political nightmare, and cloud unit Azure was growing consistently ahead of expectations. Then, the ground underneath Microsoft started to shift. On its fiscal 2026 first-quarter earnings call in October 2025, CFO Amy Hood said its capital expenditure growth rate in that fiscal year would exceed that of the prior year. Previously, Hood had signaled for a slowdown in capex growth. Shares fell 2.9% in that first session post-earnings. The reaction signaled that investors were growing increasingly concerned that revenue tied to the capex spending wasn't showing up fast enough to be comfortable with the projected level of outlays. It didn't help that over the 2025 holiday season, Anthropic's Claude Code went viral on the back of the Opus 4.5 model release. This much-more capable version of the code-writing tool further brandished Anthropic's frontier image. In the process, it made offerings like Microsoft's Copilot AI assistant seem far less attractive and therefore monetizable than hoped for. The power of Claude Code — and its Claude Cowork productivity tool — also added fuel to concerns that AI would disrupt the software industry , giving rise to the "SaaSpocalypse." The thinking was that companies could use these new coding tools to create bespoke applications internally; and even the packaged software that would survive might be threatened by AI if companies hire fewer human workers and, by extension, need fewer per-person software licenses. The fears around Microsoft's standing were on display when the company reported earnings on Jan. 28 after the closing bell. The results demonstrated that Microsoft still needed to improve its "growth-to-spending" ratio, as we noted at the time. Put another way, Microsoft was spending too much in the minds of investors and not showing enough of a payoff quickly enough. With that earnings release, we also learned that 45% of Microsoft's massive commercial backlog was from the profitless, cash-flow-negative OpenAI. That new disclosure didn't help sentiment, either. Shares tumbled 10% the following session — its biggest one-day drop since falling nearly 15% on March 16, 2020, during the early days of the pandemic. To be sure, demand was not the issue. As we wrote at the time , "Microsoft has some issues to sort out to either get more Azure capacity online or to better balance capital expenditure growth to improve margins. The recent stock decline is disappointing, but we're betting CEO Satya Nadella and CFO Amy Hood will figure it out." However, sentiment around Microsoft would get worse. A key concern: the amount of Azure computing resources that Microsoft was committing to the internal development of Copilot, which, at this point, was being viewed as a total disappointment in the face of fierce competition. There was OpenAI and Anthropic, of course. But Microsoft looked even worse now that Alphabet had gone from black sheep to market darling, thanks to the release of Gemini 3 in late 2025. The revelation that Microsoft was holding back capacity — and in turn limiting Azure revenue — for a product that wasn't even seriously in the AI conversation, made the spending concerns even more understandable. So, too, was the decline in the stock. As Melius Research analyst Ben Reitzes wrote in his Feb. 9, 2026, downgrade of Microsoft: "Due to things like Cowork from Anthropic, Microsoft's powerful 365 suite could see challenges and may need to give Copilot away just to stay relevant — hurting growth and margins in its most profitable Productivity segment. This reality will consume internal capacity of Azure, limiting beats there too. ... Azure's lack of ability to beat is inextricably linked to Copilot. If Copilot adoption and capabilities are not up to par, Microsoft needs to spend more on AI modeling and R & D and whatever else consuming internal Azure capacity for themselves. We are increasingly realizing the folly in our logic only a few weeks ago — we were worried about Copilot woes, but overlooked it because we loved Azure's prospects. If you think Copilot is a dud, it requires more investment in internal capacity since it will need to be given away. Voila - Azure can't beat because Microsoft needs the capacity for themselves - period. The linkage of these 2 issues have thus killed the Azure narrative until proven otherwise." Upstarts were encroaching on Microsoft's enterprise software turf, and not only did the company not seem to have the horses to fend them off, but it was sacrificing revenue in the process of beefing up its defenses. While management could argue that was the right long-term move, we know Wall Street loves short-term thinking. Make no mistake, we certainly expressed our frustration with Microsoft's performance throughout the spring, including after earnings in April , and into the summer. Jim Cramer was an especially vocal critic of Copilot, believing that the number of paid subscribers relative to those paying for Microsoft's broader software suite was paltry. The company's high-stakes Build conference in early June wasn't enough to lift the stock, and that month would bring widespread carnage across the broader software stock universe. Microsoft's low close of the year came on June 25 at $252.83 a share. Shares had started to perk up into July — and then came its fiscal fourth-quarter earnings report later in the month. That's when many of issues plaguing the stock started to turn around. First off, the company didn't raise its spending outlook. While that didn't necessarily speak to any improvements with Copilot development, it made clear that investors had indeed likely overshot to the downside in a panic. Moreover, Microsoft was able to bring more Azure capacity online quicker than Wall Street had excepted. That it grew its commercial backlog with customers outside of the frontier labs — in effect reducing its reliance on the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic, though that remains material — also helped sentiment. Not for nothing, the number of paying Copilot subscribers increased to over 30 million from over 20 million in April. This is also right about the time that the highly levered Situational Awareness hedge fund started to blow up, alleviating some of the negative sentiment around software. The fund, run by a former OpenAI researcher, had been a huge proponent of the "short software, long hardware" trade. That was enough to help the stock get back to the $500s in early August, even as Copilot wasn't fully figured out. Fast forward again, to late September, and we got the news that would ultimately help Microsoft reach a new all-time high. Microsoft launched a retooled version of Copilot and outlined a strategy focused on the corporate world it already dominates. Not long after, Reitzes upgraded Microsoft back to a buy rating , pointing to the overhauled Copilot strategy and emerging concerns about the reputation of the frontier labs. The lessons learned So, why did we stick with it? That's the question that really matters now, as we look to pull a lesson from this past year of Microsoft price action. First off, we had faith in management. That's not to say you should invest on hope, but it is to say that the team running a company is one of the most important factors to consider when it comes to single-stock investing. For Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and CFO Amy Hood, their track records speak for themselves. Nadella, who took over the top job in 2014, brought Microsoft into the cloud computing and software-as-a-service era , while Hood has consistently proven herself to be one of the best CFOs in the game. Hood has been Microsoft's finance chief since 2013. Second, we understood that while Microsoft was burning enormous amounts of capital to build more AI infrastructure, the spending was in its control. In other words, it was a self-inflicted "wound," and not something more concerning like a deterioration in demand. As a result, we understood that if management decided it needed to pivot, they could do so until investors got more visibility into monetization opportunities. To put it simply, this was a high-quality company that needed to prove itself again, not a company that was lucky to be successful and was now seeing its luck run out. Under Nadella, Microsoft had faced disruption before and come out stronger on the other side, benefiting from the cloud-computing revolution and the embrace of the SaaS model. Some of Jim's longstanding investment rules apply here too: Own the best of breed; it is worth it : Microsoft certainly fits the bill here for the reasons we laid out above. The management team is as good as it gets, and the company's rock-solid balance sheet is a big advantage too. Nobody ever made a dime panicking : Plenty of investors were panicking about the "SaaSpocalypse" in the first half of this year. While perhaps not as acute in shares of Microsoft versus a name like Adobe , Figma and Intuit , as the move played out, it became increasingly clear that investors were starting to overreact about potential AI disruption for enterprise software companies. While some level of concern was justified because of elevated uncertainty, the panic likely meant the move was overshooting to the downside. That the market has become so algorithmically driven — and that so many names were being bucketed into sell orders thanks to "ETFization" — also didn't help. For example, bad news out of ServiceNow didn't mean everyone sold NOW stock, it meant plenty of people dumped their software exchange-traded funds. The most prominent example is the sold the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV), which holds everything from pure-play enterprise software to cybersecurity, and yes, Microsoft (currently the third-biggest holding in the fund). Buy and homework, not buy and hold : Of course, acknowledging that there is panic in the air doesn't mean you ignore it simply because you're too cool for school. Sometimes, panic is warranted (like when the folks running the Federal Reserve "know nothing!" ) So, if you're not going to panic, you better have a good reason and you only get that by doing the homework. In the case of Microsoft, it became clear that at least some of the capacity constraint was due to that internal desire to advance Copilot. If more compute had gone to external demand, Azure growth and overall revenue would've bene better. We didn't like that that was the case, but it did mean that we were that much closer to better understanding the issue. Step one to fixing an issue, of course, is being able to identify it. With the problem better understood, we better understood what needed to be done. As such, Jim and others on Wall Street started to get more vocal about the need to turn Copilot around. When analysts and shareholders have identified a core issue they have, it's harder for management to ignore and can therefore increase their sense of urgency in addressing the issue. Patience is a virtue — giving up on value is a sin : Ultimately, it all comes back to valuation. As we watched shares decline seemingly day after day, week after week, month after month, we never lost track of the price-to-earnings multiple. As Microsoft's stock price declined, so too did its price-to-earnings multiple. This indicated to us that for all the concern being baked into the price, earnings estimates weren't being cut nearly as fast. In fact, the estimates were largely going up, according to FactSet data. So, shares really were becoming much cheaper, making the potential reward if our faith in management was rightly given, that much greater. Microsoft started the year at roughly 28 times forward earnings. By late June, it had compressed all the way to 18. Bottom line As thrilled as we are that Microsoft has clawed its way back, and as much money was made on Microsoft, far more will be made in the years to come by understanding why this call worked out. By focusing on only best-of-breed names (with some exception, like when you spot an incredible turnaround opportunity), you give yourself the best chance of making money in the future. By then doing all you can eliminate emotion from your analysis — across the spectrum, from hope to panic — you can better ensure objectivity. Of course, it's much easier to eliminate emotion when you are well-educated, so doing the homework is a non-negotiable. Finally, when you've done all that, you'll know if you're sitting on value or not. If you've got value, all there is to do is be patient. More often than not, if the analysis was correct, that patience will be rewarded, as it has been for us with Microsoft. Funny enough, without starting all over, we would argue a similar dynamic has played out with Meta in the past few weeks. And, in the interest of fairness, had we had a bit more patience with Alphabet, we would not have exited that name last year before it went on a huge run. Fortunately, we had enough awareness to acknowledge our mistake and get back in before it could climb even higher — underscoring a few other rules Jim has come to abide over his decades of experience: don't dig in your heels when you're wrong, swallow your pride. When the facts change, so too must your mind, or, at the very least, you must gut check your initial thesis. We did it with Alphabet, and while we missed last year's monster run, we still managed to get back in in time to make money. Thankfully, with Microsoft, we never left. articles.title: Anduril employee tender offer would value the defense tech startup at $90 billion
articles.text:
Defense tech startup Anduril will give employees a chance to sell stock through a tender offer that would value the company at roughly $90 billion, CNBC has confirmed.
Bloomberg was the first to report the news, citing sources familiar with the matter. Anduril confirmed the report to CNBC.
Employees participating in the offering can sell shares at $94.80 apiece. The offer, which opened on Oct. 13 and closes Nov. 9, is capped at $1.3 billion, according to the report.
Bloomberg reported that employees in 16 countries are eligible to participate.
Anduril has been a major winner of the growing U.S. defense tech boom and President Donald Trump's plans to reindustrialize the U.S. military. In May, the company closed a $5 billion funding round that doubled its valuation to $61 billion.
Co-founder and Oculus headset creator Palmer Luckey is among a growing group of defense tech leaders taking on advisory roles in Washington as they compete for key Department of Defense contracts.
This month, the company inked a U.S. Navy shipyard contract worth up to $2.9 billion, shortly after Luckey was named a co-director of Project Meridian, which aims to develop and scale military capabilities. SpaceX rocket maker CEO Elon Musk also joined the initiative.
Founded in 2017, Anduril has gained prominence for its drones, augmented reality headsets and AI software it's developing for the U.S. government and allied governments. Last month, the company made headlines after Iran said it had captured one of its underwater vehicles.

articles.title: The energy sector is taking the bull market lead from tech. Here's one way to play it
articles.text: (See the video above for Todd's complete chart breakdown.) It's hard to believe, but energy — not technology — is not only still leading the sector year-to-date scorecard in 2026, it's building on the lead. Last week, we talked about a Brazilian energy company. I was looking forward to talking technology this week, but we need to stay where the "energy" is. The Energy Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLE) is up 53.3% year to date, more than three times the S & P 500's 15% gain. The Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLK) is still up a strong 36.8%, but look at the shaded box on the right side of the chart. Over the past two weeks, tech rolled over while energy ripped to new highs. Wednesday's September CPI report added fuel. Headline inflation came in at 3.7%, a tenth above expectations, and bond yields pushed higher. That's a headwind for long-duration growth stocks and, in my view, another reason that energy has staying power. I think there's a deeper message that we need to uncover here from the bond market, more than just hot inflation or geopolitical tensions. I split the 10-year Treasury yield into its two pieces: expected inflation and real yields. Only real yields are making new highs while expected inflation remains off the highs. I also overlay crude oil on all three measures. It tracks one far more closely than the others, and that matters for how energy trades from here. There's the crude oil chart itself. Even after this week's Houthi attack on a Saudi Aramco facility, WTI is coiled in a tight triangle between falling resistance in the low 100s and rising support near 90. Whichever way it breaks should set the tone for the whole energy complex. In our latest rebalance of the portfolios, we maintained our significantly overweight allocation to energy. The cleanest play in here, in our view, is in the barrel. It's the refining margins. The diesel crack spread (what refiners earn turning crude into diesel) climbed from about $25 a barrel in January to a peak above $110 in September. It's cooled to around $95, yet the VanEck Oil Refiners ETF is holding near its highs. Marathon Petroleum This is why we re-entered Marathon Petroleum (MPC) in our most recent rebalance and why we remain overweight energy. Marathon has climbed inside a well-defined channel since its 2020 low. At about $477, it sits far above its 200-week moving average near $181. Resistance points to the $600 to $650 area, so there may be room to run. As described in the video, I'm definitely nervous about adding to this name and the energy industry, as they are so extended. But the market is telling us that energy stocks are trading on more than just inflation expectations or geopolitical pressures. There's more to the story. We, as active managers, mean staying with the trade that the market is focused on, with a defined plan in case it unwinds. Marathon reports Q3 results on November 3 before the open. In the full video, I walk through six charts, including: The bond market signal hiding inside Wednesday's CPI sell-off Which bond yield crude oil actually trades with An understanding of how the diesel crack spread is driving the refiners The breakout and breakdown levels I'm watching on WTI Discussion of managing risk on this extended refining trade Todd Gordon is the founder of Inside Edge Capital, LLC. articles.title: These stocks offer some of the best risk-adjusted upside on Wall Street
articles.text: The recent volatility in the equity markets has created some potentially attractive opportunities for investors willing to look past near-term choppiness. CNBC Pro screened the S & P 500 for stocks with some of the highest prospective risk-adjusted returns, based on Wall Street analysts' price targets and options-implied expectations for volatility over the next 12 months. The list includes tech darlings like Nvidia and Broadcom as well as Boeing and T-Mobile , along with lesser-known names that could see substantial upside if analysts' forecasts prove accurate. There's a distinct contrarian bent to the list, with many of the stocks lower over the past month even as analysts have maintained bullish price targets. The screen was inspired partly by a strategy from Goldman Sachs. It compares the potential excess return on a stock's consensus price target (over a risk-free rate), with its 12-month implied volatility. A higher ratio suggests more potential upside relative to risk, as measure by expected volatility. Wynn Resorts tops the screen, with analysts expecting the casino operator's shares to climb about 70% to reach their consensus 12-month price target. Wynn has fallen nearly 14% over the past month, but analysts are broadly positive: all 25 who cover the stock have positive ratings, according to FactSet. T-Mobile too ranks near the top. Shares in the wireless carrier have dropped nearly 16% over the past month as potential competition from StarLink, a SpaceX division, spooked investors . But Wall Street's price target has fallen only about 1%. Analysts see roughly 54% upside from current levels and the stock's comparatively modest implied volatility helps lift its risk-adjusted score. Micron Technology is another standout, with analysts forecasting nearly 70% upside to their consensus price target. The memory-chip maker's shares have been volatile recently as investors weigh AI growth against fears of a tech-driven bubble. Nvidia is an exception in the screen, having gained about 5% over the past month, while its consensus price target has remained essentially unchanged. Analysts still see more than 40% implied upside and more than 90% have a positive rating on the Jensen Huang-led chipmaker. Other technology-related names on the screen include Broadcom, Oracle , Western Digital and AppLovin . Western Digital has one of the largest potential returns on the screen, with analysts forecasting roughly 80% upside, though its elevated implied volatility makes it one of the riskier names, by that measure.

articles.title: Berkshire Hathaway heads for 10th consecutive winning day. What's driving the stock
articles.text: The stock market has been volatile of late as a cocktail of elevated oil prices and persistent inflation rattles investors. That that hasn't been the case with Berkshire Hathaway . The conglomerate's Class A shares are on track for their 10 th consecutive day of gains. That would mark their first 10-day rally since January 2018. The stock on Tuesday also hit an intraday high of $786,000 — a level not seen since Aug. 11. The $1 trillion holding company, best known for its leadership under legendary investor Warren Buffett, is up more than 5% since the streak began as investors weigh potential tailwinds for the conglomerate under Greg Abel, who took over as CEO in January. The rally also comes as Berkshire puts its massive cash reserves to work. Its most recent move is a $330 million investment in digital media company Bending Spoons . The latest infusion follows Berkshire's $600 million investment from July, when the Italy-based serial acquirer went public on the Nasdaq. Berkshire has also grown its stake in homebuilder Lennar and now more than 13% of shares outstanding, per FactSet. BRK.A mountain 2026-10-01 BRK.A stock performance month-to-date. A contributing factor to the stock's recent strength could be higher short-term interest rates, according to Meyer Shields, analyst at Keefe, Bruyette & Woods. He noted that the company is flush with cash, "a good symbol of continued patience under the new CEO," Shields told CNBC. But it also means that if short-term interest rates go up, "they'll be making more money." The 2-year Treasury yield pulled back from its peak of 4.9% in late September and currently sits around 4.80%. Berkshire, as a major player in the insurance space, could also benefit from "no hurricane landfalls in the third quarter," Shields said, suggesting that the reassessment and potential limiting of overall catastrophe reinsurance results "worked out in their favor." Fluctuations in oil prices could be another factor in Berkshire's favor since the firm has a diverse set of investments in the energy space under its global energy holding company, Berkshire Hathaway Energy, Shields said. The winning streak comes nearly a month after Buffett officially stepped down as chairman on Sept. 18, succeeded by his son, Howard. Warren Buffett now serves as chairman emeritus of Berkshire.

articles.title: Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to patch software flaws exposed by Anthropic's Mythos
articles.text:
Bank of America has hired an army of external contractors to help it patch software vulnerabilities exposed by advanced artificial intelligence models including Anthropic's Mythos, the bank's CEO, Brian Moynihan, told CNBC on Wednesday.
In an interview after the bank's third-quarter earnings release, Moynihan said that earlier this year the company rushed to bolster a wide spectrum of its internal and vendor code using thousands of employees and outside personnel.
"That risk is real risk, and that's why when the frontier-type models came out. … A lot of us sat down and said, 'How do we figure out how to get through this quickly?" Moynihan told CNBC's Leslie Picker.
"We put on 1,000 contractors to help us do the patching work in the second quarter, and those people remain here today, helping us, on top of the 3,000 people we have in that area," he said.
The bank spent a "couple hundred million plus" on the software remediation and regulatory issues related to anti-money laundering compliance in the third quarter, Moynihan told analysts earlier Wednesday.
The comments are some of the first by a major U.S. corporation to specify the manpower and dollars spent to protect software systems from Mythos, which was released to a small group of banks, technology firms and government agencies in April.
They also highlight the dual-edged nature of AI: While it can help companies save money by boosting productivity, the ability of models like Mythos to uncover and exploit decades-old software flaws has also forced firms into a costly defensive scramble.
"We've got to stay ahead of them, and we've got to be mindful that the people doing the software development are the people trying to sell us the services," Moynihan said.
Still, Moynihan — speaking as his company's shares slumped as much as 8% Wednesday — sought to reassure investors that the spending increase was temporary.
"Once you patch, you don't have to patch as much. … The pipeline moves through," Moynihan said, adding that the bank expects remediation costs to decline over time.
In other places, AI is helping to reduce expenses. Bank of America has about 130 internal AI projects, and savings from those efforts are expected to rise from $300 million this year to $700 million in 2027, Moynihan told analysts.
Bank of America's head count fell by about 3,400 employees in the past year as the firm cut roughly 5% of managers, he said. It's unclear how much of that workforce reduction is attributable to AI.

articles.title: AI infrastructure stocks tumble. Here's a few reasons for the sell-off
articles.text: Every weekday, the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer releases the Homestretch — an actionable afternoon update, just in time for the last hour of trading on Wall Street. AI stocks are leading the market lower Wednesday after the September consumer price index came in hotter than expected. Headline CPI increased 3.7% year over year, while the ex-food and energy core rate gained 2.6%. Looking month-over-month, headline CPI rose 0.6% on a seasonally adjusted basis, with over half of the all-items increase tied to a 9.1% gain in the gasoline component. This illustrates the inflationary pressure stemming from the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, particularly through higher energy prices. The Nasdaq is down 2% in late afternoon trading, while the S & P 500 dropped more than 1% Bond prices initially sold off on the print, sending yields sharply higher. (Later in the day, yields reversed slightly into the red.) According to the CME FedWatch tool, the market odds of an interest rate rise at the central bank's upcoming October meeting increased to roughly 37% for a 25-basis-point rate hike, up from 22% on Tuesday and about 18% one week ago. More rate hikes could slow down the economy, explaining why investors are rotating into defensives within healthcare and consumer staples, and out of economically sensitive areas like banks and industrials. Tech stocks are getting hit, too. The prospects of more rate hikes played into our decision earlier in the day to exit Honeywell Technologies and build back some cash. AI infrastructure names could hit a slow patch if the cost of capital rises too quickly. Stocks like GE Vernova and Eaton were some of the biggest laggards in the portfolio Wednesday. Broadcom CEO Hock Tan warned on Monday at a conference in Singapore that access to capital could become the next industry constraint. Semiconductor stocks remained a source of market pain. The iShares Semiconductor ETF, or SOXX, fell another 4% on Wednesday, extending its losing streak to seven consecutive sessions and bringing its total decline over that stretch to nearly 12%. This is the worst SOXX losing streak since May 2025. The last time the SOXX fell for eight sessions in a row was September 2015. One more development to watch: Anthropic is expected to share its updated financials with a group of institutional investors on Wednesday. While there have been no leaked numbers yet, the market action suggests to us that there could be some disappointment. If we do see better-than-expected financials from the AI lab, that could take some of the pressure off chip stocks and other AI infrastructure-related names. Truist initiated coverage of Qnity with a buy rating and a $170-per-share price target, implying 38% upside to Tuesday's closing price of just under $123 per share. The analysts said the $25 billion market cap company's array of materials for chip manufacturing and packaging is "supportive of durable above-market growth." The bullish call followed a Barclays initiation and $211 price target on Monday. It also started Qnity with a buy rating alongside several other U.S. chemical companies, including fellow Club names DuPont and Linde . It's good to see Qnity get more positive analyst coverage, though we would prefer technology- and semiconductor-focused analysts write about it more often. We haven't forgotten about Qnity, which has fallen about 8% since the end of July and 31% from its June high. But the stock often trades with semiconductor capital equipment stocks like Applied Materials and Lam Research , and the portfolio has plenty of semiconductor exposure via Nvidia , Intel , Micron , and Broadcom. Watch our video tour of Qnity's labs outside Boston to see why the company is so important to the chip industry supply chain. There are no major earnings after the bell . On the data side, Thursday brings September retail sales and the second part of the government's inflation series, the September producer price index.
